title: Origami memory stack: one thin membrane folded into N layers, wired through the folds [SPECULATIVE]
idea: Build N memory die images side by side as one continuous thin membrane (an oxide-cell array plus 3-4 metal levels, ~1.5-3 um thick) on a glass carrier with a laser-release layer, wiring neighbouring dies together across the gaps with ordinary BEOL lines. Release the membrane and fold it accordion-style into an N-layer stack bonded with thin adhesive, with fold radii of ~150-300 um. Vertical connectivity is the BEOL wiring that runs continuously around each fold, so there are no TSVs, no micro-bumps and no die-to-die alignment. The folded stack lands on a logic base die like HBM.
why: [SPECULATIVE] HBM-like stacks at near-planar wafer cost per bit: stacking tax 3x -> ~1.05-1.1x (fold loss 4.5-8.6%), with 20,000+ vertical wires per fold.
note: Fold-routed BEOL wires replace TSVs and alignment entirely; doubts: dielectric cracking at folds, heat through adhesive, membrane yield.

title: Compute embeddings from hashes instead of storing terabyte tables
idea: Recommendation embedding tables are terabytes of mostly cold rows hit by random gathers. Replace lookup with deep-hash embedding: k hashes of the ID feed a small on-accelerator MLP that synthesizes the vector, while only the hottest ~1% of IDs stay in an explicit cache.
why: Table memory falls 100-1000x and random-gather traffic disappears; trades compute and some accuracy.
note: Known art (DHE, TT-Rec); 100x+ recsys table shrink if accuracy holds, trading compute for DRAM.

title: Mycologist's spores: hibernate idle AI agents as compressed snapshots
idea: Fungi survive lean times as tiny spores. Agent sessions spend most of their wall-clock time waiting on users or tools. After ~2 s idle, the session's KV cache, runtime heap and sandbox are snapshotted into a compressed, deduplicated spore on NVMe and rehydrated in tens of ms by lazily paging in only the pages touched first.
why: Agent fleets keep thousands of mostly idle sessions resident. Spores cut resident DRAM/HBM per concurrent agent 10-20x.
note: Insight: agent sessions idle most of wall-clock time; snapshotting KV and heap to NVMe cuts resident memory per agent ~10x.

title: Swap per-bit access transistors for vertical CCD charge-packet strings
idea: Reuse the 3D NAND stack: each vertical poly or IGZO channel works as a CCD in which the 128 tier gates, clocked in three phases, shift ~40 charge packets up and down to a regenerating sense amplifier at the top. There is no contact, capacitor or access transistor per bit, and each pass through the amplifier refreshes the packet.
why: ~1 bit per 250 nm2 (better than 864 nm2 for 6F2) using only DUV 3D NAND tools (facts 2, 4, 7); no tunnelling, so endurance is unlimited; average shift latency is ~20 ns.
note: DRAM-class bits on 3D-NAND tooling, which could give ~10x cost/bit; poly/IGZO trap CTI, dark current and clock CV2 power are the doubts.

title: Plated-pillar memory: circumferential magnetization lining 3D NAND-style holes
idea: Revive Univac/Bell plated-wire memory vertically: etch high-AR holes through a stack of word-strap tiers, ALD a soft magnetic shell, spacer and reference layer down each hole, and store bits as circumferentially magnetized ring segments under each strap, sensed non-destructively by the magnetoresistance of an axial read current. Closed-flux rings have no stray field, so hole pitch can be tight.
why: Facts 2 and 8: a deposition-built 3D cell with non-destructive read, no capacitor and near-unlimited endurance; 3D NAND-like density at ~20-50 ns reads.
note: Deposition-built 3D cell with NDRO and unlimited endurance at NAND density; ALD magnetic quality and tiny MR signal are the doubts.

title: Vertical CCD strings in a 3D-NAND stack, four phase contacts
idea: Revive 1970s CCD serial memory (Fairchild F464, Intel 2416), which needed no contact or access transistor per bit, as vertical charge-coupled strings: a 3D-NAND-style alternating oxide/gate stack is etched once for channel holes, and every fourth gate layer is tied to the same clock phase so charge packets march up the hole to a sense node at the top. With only four phase lines, the staircase and per-tier contacts disappear.
why: Fact 2 and capital: one critical hole mask for ~200 tiers, no staircase (10+ masks and trims in 3D NAND) and no capacitor pillar; shifting at ~2 GHz gives ~50 ns average latency, and recirculation doubles as refresh. Risk is charge-transfer efficiency and dark current in a deposited channel liner.
note: One hole mask for 200 tiers, no staircase or capacitor; charge-transfer efficiency and dark current in deposited liners are the doubt.

title: Diode-steered capacitor stack: one transistor, sixteen bits per pillar
idea: IFR: one switch serves a whole tower of bits. Deposit 16 plate-electrode/dielectric tiers around one vertical storage pillar, with a thin oxide Schottky diode in each tier between plate and capacitor, so a plate-line pulse forward-biases only the selected tier onto the shared pillar node, read through a single access transistor; tiers come from deposition and one hole etch.
why: Constraint: 16 bits per 4F^2 footprint is ~24x the bits of 6F^2 planar at ~1.5-2x wafer cost, about 10x bits per dollar; it also removes 15 of 16 access transistors and their leakage tail.
note: 16 bits per pillar from deposition plus one hole etch; doubt: ~0.2 fF per tier capacitance and diode disturb on shared node.

title: Thermally drawn preform ribbons shrink centimeter laminates into nanoscale cells
idea: Ideal: draw memory like optical fiber, kilometers at a time. Closest: stack a cm-scale preform of glass, oxide semiconductor and low-melting metal (Sn-Zn or Al alloy) laminates in a cell cross-section, thermally draw it 1000-10,000x into ribbons whose layers shrink to 10-50 nm, then cut and tile ribbons orthogonally into crossbar or gain-cell tiers.
why: 100x: draw towers produce km/hour at ~$0.01/m and define features by geometric draw-down, not lithography; a speculative >=100x $/GB path from abundant glass, oxide and metal. Trades interlayer diffusion during draw, coarse tiling contacts and unproven semiconductor quality.
note: Geometric draw-down replaces litho; doubts: capillary breakup of 10-50 nm layers, semiconductor quality after draw, crossbar contact alignment.

title: CDN edge caching: weak memory tier holds only clean data
idea: Adapted from CDNs, which can lose a cached object because the origin always has a copy: the OS places only clean, file-backed pages (page cache, read-only model files, container images) on a pool of cheap low-grade DRAM with detection-only codes, and any detected error simply invalidates the page and refetches it from SSD.
why: Cost per bit (facts 3, 4): page cache is often 30-60% of server memory; serving it from salvaged or relaxed-spec DRAM frees premium DRAM for dirty data, and an error costs a ~50 us refetch instead of a crash.

title: Typing-indicator KV prefetch for hibernated chat sessions
idea: When a response finishes, the server spills that session's KV cache to NVMe/CXL flash. It prefetches the cache back into HBM when the client sends a 'user started typing' or 'tab focused' event. This jumps from the nanosecond scale of HBM to the 5-60 s of human think time between turns, which hides a 10-200 ms restore completely.
why: HBM capacity and data movement (fact 5): live chat sessions are idle more than 90% of wall-clock time, yet their KV dominates inference HBM. Keeping only the actively decoding sessions resident cuts resident KV bytes about 5-15x.
note: KV offload known (LMCache, Mooncake); typing-signal prefetch is the twist.

title: Fiber-drawn salami capacitor arrays sliced into wafers
idea: Imposed scarcity: no lithography and no high-AR etch. Assemble a glass preform of millimetre metal-cored, glass-clad coaxial rods, thermally draw and restack-redraw it (as photonic-crystal fiber makers do) until cores reach ~50 nm pitch, then slice the fused bundle into 5 um discs and hybrid-bond them to a CMOS access-transistor wafer.
why: Feature size comes from draw ratio, not EUV; each slice is a sheet of billions of coaxial capacitors with AR ~100 at no etch cost, made from glass and common metals.
note: Pitch from draw ratio, no litho/etch; doubt: draw disorder breaks registration to access transistors and glass dielectric gives low Cs.

title: Minify tier thickness to 6 nm for 1000-tier atomic stacks
idea: Grow alternating MOCVD 2D-semiconductor channel sheets (MoS2 or WSe2, about 1 nm) and hBN/oxide spacers (about 5 nm) so each tier is 6 nm and 1000 tiers fit in a 6 um stack. Gain-cell storage nodes are gated by shared vertical gate holes etched once per 100-tier deck, as in 3D NAND.
why: 3D break-even (26+ tiers): goes 40x past it at a stack height that an etcher can already reach; the wide bandgap of 2D channels also cuts leakage, so refresh could fall by more than 100x.
note: 1000 tiers at 6 nm pitch would be far past 10x density; doubt: sequential 2D growth/transfer yield.

title: Composite: silicon sense chiplets mass-transferred onto glass DRAM panels
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: large glass panels carry stacked oxide-TFT DRAM tiers, while all precision sensing lives in 50x50 um silicon sense chiplets placed every few millimetres by micro-LED-style mass transfer (millions per hour) and wired by panel redistribution layers; glass does storage, silicon does amplification.
why: 100x path: panel processing costs ~$100-300/m2 versus ~$100k/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so with ~0.3 um panel nanoimprint and 16-32 TFT tiers it aims at ~$0.1-0.5/GB; trade-offs: bulky modules, ~us latency and higher energy. Speculative because panel lithography must improve ~5x. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.
note: Multi-tier oxide-TFT DRAM on cheap glass with silicon sense chiplets could hit >10x cost/bit; panel lithography, overlay, us latency doubtful.

title: Vertical charge-coupled memory: no switch per bit, just moving charge
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs its own access transistor': deposit a 200-layer gate/oxide stack (NAND-style, one hole etch), line each hole with a poly-Si or oxide channel, and clock the layer gates in 3 phases so charge packets march along the hole like a vertical CCD. Each hole holds ~60 bits and one sense/regeneration stage at the top restores packets as they circulate, so refresh is continuous and free.
why: No per-bit transistor, capacitor or litho: cost tracks 3D NAND (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x below DRAM per GB; trade-off is serial access (~us to the far bit, high streaming bandwidth) and transfer-loss risk in poly channels.
note: CCD clocking in a NAND-style stack removes per-bit transistors and capacitors; poly-channel transfer efficiency and serial latency are the doubts.

title: Papermaker's book: roll-to-roll foil memory laminated 800 sheets deep
idea: A papermaker makes thick books from cheap sheets. Print single-tier oxide-TFT gain-cell memory on 10 um polyimide foil by roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~100 nm rules, then laminate ~800 sheets per cm with anisotropic conductive film and edge-plated through-stack bus lines into a memory 'book'.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: ~60 MB/cm^2 per sheet times 800 sheets is ~50 GB/cm^3, versus ~2 GB/cm^3 for a DIMM. Roll-to-roll costs (~$20-50/m^2 per sheet) keep cost per module flat; sheet alignment and yield are the risks.
note: If 800 laminated R2R TFT sheets yield, cost/GB falls >10x; sheet yield, alignment and through-stack interconnect are near-miraculous.

title: 3D-NAND toolset builds channel-hole gain cells with no EUV
idea: Ideal: density from tier count with tools already paid for. Closest: in a NAND-style oxide/word-plate stack, each channel hole holds two concentric ALD oxide-semiconductor devices per tier: an outer write channel charging an isolated metal ring, and an inner read channel gated by that ring, so every tier crossing is a capacitorless 2T gain cell built with the 3D NAND etch, ALD and staircase flow.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 100+ tiers at DUV pitch in existing NAND fabs with no capacitor and no EUV; bit cost could follow NAND-like layer economics if speed and retention hold.
note: Concentric write/read oxide devices per channel hole gives NAND-like layer economics; doubt: IGZO speed, ring isolation, retention at tier pitch.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers as one-dimensional memory substrates
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: replace the 2D wafer with a 1D substrate. A macroscopic preform of chalcogenide-glass semiconductor, polymer dielectric and metal electrodes is thermally drawn into kilometres of fiber whose cross-section is one memory column (bitline, storage electrodes, access channel); fibers are then woven or laminated with orthogonal wordline fibers into 3D blocks.
why: Capital intensity (Fact 4): draw towers make kilometres per hour with no lithography, and wide-gap chalcogenides give low leakage (Fact 3); density and speed are highly speculative.
note: Litho-free km-scale drawn fiber columns woven into 3D blocks; doubt: fiber feature sizes and chalcogenide speed far from DRAM density.

title: Carrier-is-memory: the mandatory carrier wafer of backside-power logic becomes a DRAM wafer
idea: In backside power delivery the finished front-side BEOL is flipped and bonded to a carrier wafer, the original substrate is ground away and power is wired in from the back, so the front-side signal wiring ends up facing the carrier. Replace that blank carrier with a full DRAM wafer (1-beta-class 1T1C or an oxide-cell wafer) whose die map matches the logic reticle, and make the bond a Cu-SiCN hybrid bond at 1-2 um pitch instead of a plain dielectric fusion bond. The memory die keeps its sense amps and bank logic but drops pads, PHYs and TSVs; commands, data and memory power cross the bond. The memory wafer stays thick and becomes the heat-spreading side of the stack (pair with B3-03). For a wafer-scale engine, the same move puts a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer (~3.9 TB) under the compute wafer.
why: Memory interface energy ~12x lower (3.5 -> ~0.28 pJ/bit), saving ~200-410 W per accelerator at 8-16 TB/s; 45-53 GB per 800 mm2 logic die with zero added footprint and no HBM stacking; ~$1.7-2.3/GB of added memory at DRAM-wafer cost.
note: Backside-power carrier wafer is mandatory anyway; making it DRAM gives ~12x lower interface energy at zero footprint. Doubt: logic-DRAM die-map and yield coupling.

title: Gist tokens replace old context; raw chunks re-expand from flash
idea: Box: summarize × agent runtime × document chunk × leaves recent window × raw tokens on SSD. Older chunks are replaced by a few learned gist tokens' KV; if attention to a gist crosses a threshold the runtime re-prefills the original chunk from flash (zoom-in).
why: Million-token agents carry enormous KV; gist plus zoom keeps it ~20× smaller with recoverable fidelity.
note: Gist KV plus attention-triggered re-prefill could cut agent KV ~20x; doubt: gist fidelity and re-prefill latency spikes.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM holding year-frozen foundation model weights
idea: A standard base die, built on a DRAM-periphery or mature logic process, adds one contact/via mask that encodes a frozen model's weights as present or absent vias. Each bit takes about 2-4 F^2 and needs no capacitor and no refresh. The dies stack HBM-style beside the accelerator, and each new model release costs just that one mask. The time-scale insight: weights stay unchanged for 6-18 months, so they need no rewritable cells.
why: Weights (30-60% of inference HBM) leave DRAM entirely. A ROM bit costs about 3x less than a DRAM bit and needs no refresh energy, all for one added mask per model version.
note: One added via mask moves frozen weights out of HBM, no refresh; doubt is model churn vs 6-18 month freeze and Taalas-style prior art.

title: Genome Project biologist: open atlas of real memory contents
idea: Biology took off once the genome was sequenced. An opt-in agent samples hashed, entropy-profiled page snapshots (never raw data) from volunteer fleets and publishes a 'memory atlas': the share of zero pages, duplicates, near-duplicates, compressible types, pointer density and cold data by workload. About $800k.
why: Outside three hyperscalers, nobody knows where the reclaimable bytes are. The atlas aims every compression, dedup and tiering effort at the biggest wins, priming 20-40% savings.

title: Cross-finetune KV sharing below the first modified layer
idea: Imposed limit: a system prompt's KV may be stored once across all model variants. The platform requires finetunes to freeze the bottom k layers; those layers' KV is then bit-identical to the base model's, so every variant shares one prefix-KV store for the frozen layers and keeps private KV only for the layers it changed.
why: Serving hundreds of finetunes duplicates prefix KV; sharing the frozen layers' KV cuts that 2-5x, depending on how many layers are frozen.

title: Epigenetic masks: tenant model variants as methylation over shared base
idea: Like methylation silencing genes without changing DNA, each customer fine-tune is stored as a sparse binary mask plus per-row scales over one shared base model, applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel instead of keeping a full copy.
why: Serving 1,000 variants needs one base plus ~1/16-size masks each instead of 1,000 copies; order-of-magnitude weight-memory savings in multi-tenant serving.
note: Insight: BitDelta-style 1-bit masks over a shared base give ~10x+ savings for multi-tenant full fine-tunes; LoRA already covers many cases.

title: Landmark keys in DRAM, full KV blocks indexed on flash
idea: Inverts 'attention needs every past token resident': DRAM keeps one landmark key per 64-token block, and the full KV blocks sit on NVMe/CXL flash. Each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks whose landmarks score highest against the query.
why: Million-token contexts need DRAM for only ~2-5% of their KV: a 20-50x cut in KV DRAM.
note: Landmark/Quest-style top-k block retrieval puts 95%+ of long-context KV on flash; widely pursued, so low novelty.

title: Gen-8.5 display glass replaces 300 mm wafers for capacity memory
idea: Substitute DRAM fabs with idle LCD/OLED backplane lines: use their IGZO TFT process on 2.2x2.5 m glass to build 4-8 stacked layers of relaxed-pitch (~0.8 um) oxide-semiconductor gain-cell arrays, dice into large memory tiles with a bonded small CMOS controller, and sell as CXL far-memory modules.
why: Capital intensity and EUV (fact 4): depreciated display capex, zero EUV, new supply outside the DRAM-fab bottleneck; ~30-50 GB per layer per panel, roughly $8-15/GB at 4-8 layers, competitive at today's 4x prices for a slower ~100-300 ns tier.
note: Depreciated Gen-8.5 IGZO lines add EUV-free capacity; doubt: 0.8 um pitch density and slow tier may not hold $/GB long term.

title: Swap per-GPU weight copies for an optical weight-broadcast tree
idea: Substitute storage with broadcast. Instead of every accelerator keeping its own copy of the model weights in HBM, a central weight store streams each layer's weights over a WDM optical broadcast tree, timed to the synchronized decode step, so each of N accelerators buffers only the 1-2 layers in flight in SRAM. HBM is left for KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are copied 8-64x across a serving pod. One copy plus broadcast (~1.4 TB/s for a 70B fp8 model at 20 steps/s) cuts weight-resident HBM ~Nx, freeing 50-90% of HBM in weight-dominated serving. Attacks the HBM TSV tax and capital intensity.
note: One weight copy streamed per decode step frees most weight-resident HBM; doubt: ~1.4 TB/s optical receive per accelerator and strict lockstep.

title: CCD imager registers: vertical charge-shift strings replace capacitors
idea: Adapted from CCD image sensors: a 3D gate stack wrapped around a vertical silicon or oxide-semiconductor channel stores bits as charge packets in potential wells under each gate tier; a read clocks packets down the string to a floating-diffusion sense node at the base, like a CCD vertical register.
why: Removes both 3D blockers, the capacitor and the lateral transistor (fact 2); ~4F2/N per bit with NAND-like one-litho-for-all-tiers cost; trade-off ~50-100 ns serial shift for 32-tier strings.
note: NAND-like one-litho tiers with no capacitor; doubt: serial-only access, transfer losses, destructive string read.

title: Teletext data carousel: broadcast weights to accelerators that store nothing
idea: Borrowed from broadcast TV data carousels that loop content for any receiver to catch: a rack-level weight server streams the model layer by layer in a continuous optical multicast loop from ROM/NAND, and every accelerator computes on each layer as it passes, aligning its batches to the carousel phase.
why: N accelerators share one non-volatile copy of weights with zero weight DRAM and zero refresh; per-accelerator DRAM shrinks to KV only.
note: N accelerators share one streamed weight copy; doubt: batch-phase alignment and latency, Cerebras-style weight streaming partly known.

title: Idle display fabs print stacked oxide-TFT memory panels
idea: Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED fabs (2.2 x 2.5 m glass, 1.5-2 um lithography, mature IGZO TFT know-how) sit in overcapacity. Retool them to build 4-8 BEOL-stacked oxide-TFT gain-cell memory layers on glass panels, dice panels into tiles, and attach them through a CXL controller as a ~100-300 ns capacity tier.
why: One panel has ~75x the area of a 300 mm wafer; at 2 um rules and 6 stacked layers that is ~100+ GB per panel on depreciated tools with no EUV, crystal growth or quartz crucibles, potentially undercutting 4x-inflated DRAM $/GB for capacity tiers.
note: Depreciated Gen-8.5 glass area at 2um rules; doubt: ~10-50 GB/panel, panel-tile interconnect and yield may erase $/GB edge.

title: Memory on window glass: multi-tier oxide TFT cells on display lines
idea: Inverts 'memory is made on 300 mm silicon wafers': run 1T1C cells on idle Gen-8.5 to Gen-10.5 LCD/OLED glass lines, stacking 10-20 tiers with KrF-class litho at ~0.3 um and oxide-TFT access whose ultralow leakage lets tiny capacitors skip refresh; dice panels into tiles bonded to a small CMOS controller.
why: Display glass costs ~100-1000x less per area than leading-edge silicon; at 20 tiers and 4F2, ~$0.1-0.4/GB, ~25-100x cheaper; trade-off is ~100 ns-1 us access and lower density per volume.
note: Gen-10.5 glass is cheap per area; 20 tiers at 0.3 um could approach <$0.5/GB, but 100 ns-1 us access makes it capacity-tier, not DRAM.

title: Thousand-times-leakier cells tamed by a refresh engine per tile
idea: Inverts 'access transistors must leak <=13 fA': use the cheapest stackable access devices (unannealed sputtered poly-Si or oxide TFTs leaking ~10 pA) so retention is only ~10-100 us, and put a micro-sense-amp under each 4k-cell tile (CMOS-under-array) that refreshes its own tile continuously without touching global bitlines.
why: Trades refresh energy (~3-5x today) for ~100x lower cost per GB from low-temperature, 2-mask tiers with no deep capacitor; refresh traffic never leaves the tile, so bandwidth is unaffected.
note: Cheap stacked TFT tiers; doubt: 1000x refresh rate makes standby energy dominant.

title: Open array-to-periphery bond standard for merchant cell wafers
idea: Inverting 'one company makes the whole DRAM die': publish an open hybrid-bond interface (bitline pitch, preamp spec, power and test pads) so array fabs sell bare cell wafers and many periphery designers, including US logic foundries, sell sense/decode dies, like UCIe for memory internals.
why: Splits the $15B integrated fab into an array-only fab plus commodity logic, lowering capital intensity and entry barriers; the US can take periphery share immediately.
note: Disaggregates array and periphery fabs; doubt: bitline-pitch bonding needs tight co-design, hard to commoditize.

title: One optical copy of weights broadcast to a hundred accelerators
idea: First principles: read-only weights need O(1) storage, not O(N) copies, if broadcast bandwidth exists. Keep one model copy in a central memory node and stream it in layer order through a passive 1:128 optical splitter tree to accelerators running in lockstep; each holds only a few-layer SRAM ring buffer.
why: Weight GB per accelerator falls ~100x, so cost per served GB ~100x lower; trades scheduling flexibility (all nodes run the same layer at once).
note: One weight copy streamed to many lockstep accelerators; broadcast bandwidth, splitter loss and lockstep scheduling are doubts.

title: Po: the worst transistor is the best — cryo poly-Si 3D stack
idea: Po: the worst transistor is the best. Extracted: build 128-tier 1T1C stacks with cheap, leaky low-temperature poly-Si TFT access devices using a NAND-like single-hole etch and no EUV, then run the module at ~150 K where trap-assisted leakage drops by orders of magnitude, turning unusable cells into seconds-retention DRAM.
why: Accepting a cryocooler unlocks the cheapest 3D flow (near NAND cost, ~100x below DRAM contract) and also lowers wire resistance. Trade-offs: cooling power and cold packaging.
note: Cryo rescues leaky NAND-style 3D 1T1C; doubt: field-enhanced trap tunneling and GIDL do not freeze out, plus cooling overhead.

title: Ephemeral RAM: leaky poly-Si cells for data that dies young
idea: IFR: the data dies before the bit does. Define an ephemeral memory class with 0.5-2 ms retention made of cheap, leaky poly-Si 2T0C gain cells stacked in NAND-style tiers, and have the accelerator runtime map only activations, gradients and KV blocks with measured lifetimes under a millisecond onto it, so refresh is never issued.
why: Constraint: accepting poor leakage buys NAND-like stacking cost, >10x density at about the same wafer cost, with zero refresh for the large short-lived share of accelerator traffic.
note: Accept ms retention to get cheap stacked poly-Si gain cells for short-lived AI data; doubt: 2T0C NAND-like stacking density claim.

title: Interposer-as-memory: oxide DRAM tiers in the passive interposer
idea: Under 400 C, build four oxide-channel 1T1C DRAM tiers in the BEOL of the large passive silicon interposer that already sits under the GPU and HBM, patterned with ArF at 40 nm. The interposer becomes about 100 GB of near memory directly under the compute die.
why: Facts 5 and 6: about 150 Mb per mm2 per tier on about 2500 mm2 of otherwise idle silicon, sub-pJ/bit access, no TSVs and no extra wafer.
note: Idle interposer BEOL becomes ~100 GB near memory at sub-pJ/bit; doubt: oxide 1T1C density at 40 nm and interposer cost.

title: ESCO shared-savings contracts for reclaiming cold DRAM pages
idea: Like energy-service companies paid from a client's utility savings, a vendor installs a page-temperature profiler and transparent tiering agent that moves cold pages to compressed or CXL far memory, and is paid a fixed share of the DRAM purchases the customer avoids.
why: Typical enterprise servers keep 30-50% cold pages; zero-upfront contracts make adoption fast, cutting new DRAM buying by 20-30%.

title: Via-ROM for frozen AI weights: nothing to refresh
idea: Inverts 'working memory must be rewritable': store fixed model weights as present/absent or size-coded (2-bit) vias in a dense crosspoint read-only array using two custom mask layers on a mature node; changing the model re-spins only the via mask, and only activations use DRAM.
why: Zero refresh power with no capacitor, high-k or tungsten pillars; frees 50-80% of inference DRAM/HBM at 2-4 bits per F2.
note: Hardwired weights proven concept; useful only for frozen models, re-spin cost per model update.

title: Reclaimed server DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Substitute new DRAM purchases with DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs pulled from decommissioned servers: a small team builds an FPGA or off-the-shelf CXL-controller card holding 8-16 used DIMMs, screens them with an on-card pattern tester, and sells them as CXL Type-3 capacity tiers.
why: Cost per bit and scarcity: reused bits cost ~10-20% of new ones and add supply with zero fab capex during the 4x price spike.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL; supply bounded by retirement volume.

title: Bit-plane memory layout for progressive-precision fetch
idea: MINIFY bits moved by storing tensors bit-plane by bit-plane (all MSBs together, then the next plane, and so on), so an accelerator fetches only the top N planes that the current layer or token needs.
why: Data-movement energy and effective capacity: 2-4x fewer bits moved for inference, with precision chosen per access.
note: Bit-plane / progressive-precision layouts are published; software and FPGA demo easy.

title: Taking out: cold MoE experts moved to router-ahead prefetched DDR4 tier
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the cold mass: mixture-of-experts models keep only routed-hot experts in HBM, and the rest live in commodity DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL controllers. A tiny predictor runs the next layer's router one layer early so the needed experts stream over CXL before they are used. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less HBM: 2-4x less HBM per accelerator for MoE inference, shifting capacity to cheap trailing-node DRAM.
note: Known art: Pre-gated MoE, MoE-Infinity.

title: Map-tile mipmapped KV cache: zoom only where needed
idea: Map apps load coarse tiles, then zoom in. Keep pooled summary keys for each 64-token block in HBM and score those blocks first. Full-resolution KV blocks come from CXL or flash only for the highest-scoring tiles.
why: Long-context KV caches fill most of HBM. Tile-based fetch could shrink the HBM KV footprint 4-8x with little accuracy loss.
note: Quest/InfLLM-style block summary keys already published.

title: Idle chat sessions keep tokens, not KV caches, until resumed
idea: A KV entry is ~100-500 KB per token but the token that produced it is 2 bytes, and most KV memory belongs to sessions idle between user turns. Evict idle sessions to token IDs only and re-prefill them on return using cheap older-node recompute chiplets, trading FLOPs for bytes.
why: Resident KV memory falls 100x+ for typical chat duty cycles; trades resume latency and prefill energy.

title: Paper airplane: bit-plane layout so reads fetch only needed precision
idea: A paper airplane flies with only what it needs: weights are stored transposed into bit-planes, so a 4-bit inference pass reads only the top 4 planes of FP16 weights over the link. Implemented as a controller and layout change on an FPGA prototype.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth: 2-4x fewer bits moved per inference, and one stored copy serves many precisions.
note: Bit-plane and any-precision weight layouts already published.

title: Swap fixed-precision KV for age-graded fading precision
idea: Substitute uniform precision with human-like memory decay. KV entries are written at 8 bits; a background kernel requantizes them to 4 bits after ~1k tokens and 2 bits after ~8k, then evicts them, unless their cumulative attention mass marks them salient. This is pure software on unchanged HBM.
why: Long contexts average about 3 bits per element instead of 16, a ~5x KV cut that keeps important tokens sharp.

title: Hashed compositional embeddings plus a learned head cache
idea: Combine the hashing trick (each ID composes its vector from several shared sub-tables via independent hashes) with a small table of fully learned rows for the hottest IDs; IDs are promoted to full rows as their frequency rises and demoted when they cool.
why: Recommendation models hold multi-TB embedding tables in DRAM; the long tail compresses 10-50x with little accuracy loss.
note: QR/hashing-trick embeddings with frequency-based promotion are known.

title: Minify serverless memory: fork thousands from one golden snapshot
idea: Minify per-instance memory: each function runtime is pre-initialized once (imports, JIT, models loaded) and every instance forks copy-on-write from that golden snapshot in microseconds, holding only its private dirty pages (~3-8%).
why: Serverless and agent sandboxes fit 10-30x more instances per GB.
note: Firecracker/SnapStart-style COW snapshots known.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory stores replace triple replication
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: discard replicas and recover lost data from parity; in-memory caches and KV stores stripe objects RS(8,2) across servers' DRAM, with encode and decode done at line rate by a 180 nm XOR/Galois-field engine on the NIC.
why: 3x replication becomes 1.25x overhead, a ~58% DRAM saving for replicated in-memory datasets.
note: EC-Cache/Cocytus-style known art.

title: Map-tile mipmaps: multi-resolution embeddings split across DRAM and flash
idea: Like web maps loading coarse tiles before fine ones, store a 4-bit coarse version of each embedding or retrieval vector in DRAM and its residual refinement levels on flash; the model uses the coarse level by default and fetches residuals only when a confidence check fails.
why: Most lookups are satisfied at the coarse level; ~4x less DRAM for large embedding and retrieval indexes with flash serving <10% of reads.

title: Sourdough starter: persist tokens, regrow KV on demand
idea: Keep only the starter: persist each session's token IDs (2-4 bytes per token) to flash and drop its KV cache (100 KB+ per token on large models) under pressure; a cost model chooses between regrowing KV by prefill on idle compute and fetching a stored copy.
why: Persistent state shrinks ~10^4-10^5x per token; exploits compute being more abundant than memory.

title: Precision that ages: KV entries fade from FP16 to 2-bit
idea: Inverts 'a value keeps its precision for life': a background kernel demotes KV entries as they age or lose attention mass (FP16 to FP8 to INT4 to INT2), like a JPEG whose quality fades with distance, while recent and high-attention tokens stay sharp.
why: Average KV storage near 3 bits per element instead of 16: a 4-5x KV footprint cut at long context with small accuracy loss.
note: Importance/age-based KV precision (KIVI, MiKV, ZipCache) is crowded art.

title: KV cache whose precision decays with token age and attention
idea: Box: approximate × KV manager × 16-token block × age-triggered × format ladder FP16→FP8→INT4→INT2→evict. A background re-quantizer demotes blocks as they age and as their accumulated attention mass stays low, while sink tokens and recently attended blocks stay at full precision.
why: Attention mass concentrates on recent and a few anchor tokens; an average of 3–4 bits per value instead of 16 shrinks long-context KV 4–5×.

title: One model per person: users as 1-bit deltas over shared base
idea: From the extreme of a personalized model for every user: each fine-tune is stored as a sign-only 1-bit delta mask with per-matrix scales over one resident base and applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel, so millions of personal models share a single base in HBM.
why: A 1-bit delta is 16x smaller than BF16 weights and is never materialized; per-user model memory falls 16x+, and water with it.

title: Roll-to-roll web: stream tiles depth-first through every layer
idea: Activations are treated like the web in a roll-to-roll line. Each input tile runs through all layers (or a deep stage) before the next tile enters, and the overlap 'splice' halos at tile edges are recomputed. Full feature maps are never written to DRAM; only a moving web of tiles stays in on-chip SRAM. The compiler picks tile size the way a line picks web width, trading halo recompute against buffer size.
why: Activation memory for vision, diffusion and video models falls 10-50x, and DRAM traffic for intermediate tensors (fact 5) mostly disappears, at a cost of about 5-15% extra compute.

title: Benetton postponement: dye per-tenant fine-tunes at compute time
idea: Benetton knits undyed sweaters and dyes them at the last moment. One base model stays resident and serves thousands of fine-tuned variants. Each variant is stored as a 1-bit sign delta plus per-row scales (or a low-rank adapter), and the 'dye' is fused into the GEMM, so no variant is ever materialized in DRAM.
why: N full model copies become one base plus N deltas of about 1/16 the size, a 10-100x memory reduction for multi-tenant fine-tune hosting.
note: BitDelta and S-LoRA/Punica are prior art.

title: Decommissioned-server DRAM recertified by in-system retention retest
idea: Combine e-waste recycling with in-system profiling: retired DDR4/DDR5 modules pass through an automated rack that runs retention and hammer profiling, writes per-module weak-row maps into SPD and redeploys them behind stronger controller ECC as CXL-attached expansion.
why: Supply shortage: reclaims existing bits with no fab capital and US-located refurbishment, delivering usable memory at a fraction of new price.

title: Vacuum-sealed bag: FPGA CXL card compresses memory inline
idea: Stimulus 'vacuum storage bag' (same clothes, a third of the space) -> a 10-person team builds an FPGA CXL memory expander that compresses cache lines inline (LZ4/base-delta hybrid with hardware page metadata), presenting 2-3x more logical capacity than physical DRAM.
why: Does DRAM's job with about half the bits for compressible (mostly cold) data, multiplying scarce DRAM supply per card.
note: CXL compression expanders already pursued by vendors; FPGA demo straightforward.

title: Urban-mined DRAM: re-binned retired DIMM dies in CXL expanders
idea: Box [existing DDR4 die | existing access | existing sense | CXL Type-3 expander | retired server DIMMs | test + retention re-binning]: route decommissioned hyperscale DIMMs to a test line that sorts dies by retention and bit-error rate, then a CXL controller with strong ECC and per-bin refresh tuning presents them as pooled far memory.
why: Raises usable memory supply with zero new wafers, crucibles, helium or tungsten; millions of retired DIMMs per year become a far-memory tier that offsets new DDR5 demand.
note: DDR4 reuse behind CXL is already pursued by hyperscalers; retention re-binning adds modest value.

title: Retired-server DIMM reclamation business delivering tens-of-cents-per-GB pooled memory
idea: Ideal: memory that already exists and costs nothing. Closest: buy decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs from hyperscaler refresh cycles at scrap-plus prices, auto-test and grade them, and mount them on CXL Type-3 expander cards whose controllers remap weak rows and add stronger ECC, sold as pooled second-tier memory.
why: 100x: many PB retire each year; marginal cost is test + card + controller (~$0.05-0.15/GB at scale), ~50-100x below new-DRAM pricing, with zero new wafers, helium or tungsten. Trades +70-150 ns CXL latency, power and supply variability.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL; supply bounded by retirements.

title: Thousand-composition sputter library hunts for k-over-100 dielectrics
idea: MAGNIFY experiment throughput ~1000x: co-sputter three targets with deliberate thickness gradients onto one 150-mm wafer pre-patterned with 1,000 MIM test capacitors, then auto-probe k, leakage at 1 V and breakdown overnight, screening ternary oxide spaces such as Ti-Zr-La-O weekly.
why: A fast, cheap route to k >= 70 at <= 1e-7 A/cm2 (fact 1) without big-fab capital.
note: Composition-spread high-k searches date to Bell Labs 1998; cheap and fast but well-trodden.

title: Cloud DFT screen for a k-70 dielectric that ALD can grow
idea: Worsen: keep the k ~40 ZrO2 stack forever. Flip: spend ~$300k of cloud compute on a high-throughput DFT and phonon screen of rutile and alloyed oxides (Ti-Ge-Sn-O, Hf-Ti-O) for k >= 70 with band gap >= 4 eV and ALD growth below 450 C, then test the top five in a university ALD within 24 months.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): k 70 lets AR fall from 75:1 to ~45:1, a cheap route to a step change.
note: High-throughput DFT dielectric databases exist; ALD realizability of predicted phases is the doubt.

title: Clonal-selection retention profiler RTL for commodity DDR5 on FPGA
idea: Like adaptive immunity, an FPGA controller (DRAM Bender-class) 'challenges' rows with stretched refresh and worst-case patterns. Failing rows are clonally expanded into a Bloom-filter list kept at 64 ms, and negative selection re-tests them to purge false positives and catch VRT drift. Everything else refreshes at 256 ms. Three engineers for 24 months plus $80k of boards, ~$900k total, produce licensable controller RTL.
why: Fact 3: ~4x fewer refreshes for >99.9% of rows saves ~70% of refresh energy and most of the 10-20% bandwidth tax, with no DRAM die change.
note: Close to RAIDR/REAPER/AVATAR prior art; value is licensable RTL, not new mechanism.

title: Saprotroph recycling: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Saprotrophic fungi turn dead wood into new growth. An FPGA CXL Type-3 card hosts 8-16 salvaged DDR4 RDIMMs from retired servers and takes over the aged chips' 'periphery intelligence': per-DIMM retention profiling, chipkill ECC, adaptive refresh and bad-row remap, so they serve as a slower tier. One board spin plus firmware, ~$800k in 24 months, with revenue from refurbished pools.
why: Supply axis: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Reusing even 10% adds memory at ~10-20% of new DDR5 cost/bit with zero fab capex.

title: Urban-mining line requalifies retired server DRAM
idea: Inverts 'new supply needs new wafers'. Robotic hot-air reflow strips DRAM packages from retired server DIMMs, a 48-hour retention and row-hammer stress screen sorts them, and they are re-mounted on CXL memory-expander cards for pooled tiers.
why: Hundreds of millions of GB retire yearly; recovered supply at ~10-20% of new-wafer capital per GB, zero EUV.
note: CXL reuse of retired DDR4 already pursued by hyperscalers.

title: 2050 engineer: KV cache stored as per-sequence implicit neural field
idea: A 2050 engineer stores functions, not tables. For each long sequence, a tiny sinusoidal MLP per layer is fitted online to map (position, head) to the K/V vector and refitted incrementally every few hundred tokens, and attention queries this field instead of a table. Exact KV is kept only for the recent window and for outlier tokens the field reconstructs poorly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory. A 20-50x fit on older tokens would turn 1M-token contexts from hundreds of GB into a few GB. The accuracy risk is high.
note: KV as fitted implicit function could give 20-50x; doubt: K/V vectors are not smooth in position, so fits likely lossy.

title: Smoke detector: leaky analog charge counters catch row hammer
idea: Smoke builds up in an ionization chamber until the alarm trips. Give each group of 4 rows one tiny capacitor in the wordline-driver strip that gets a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks with a ~64 ms time constant; a comparator trips at ~500 activations' worth of charge and queues a targeted neighbour refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9, ~1k activation threshold): replaces SRAM counter tables and TRR logic with ~3 transistors plus 1 cap per 4 rows, monitors every row so it cannot be evaded by many-sided patterns, and costs <1% die.

title: SoftRAM 95 lesson: audited effective-GB rating for memory compression
idea: Syncronys' SoftRAM 95 sold 'RAM doubling' that did nothing, poisoning trust in memory compression for decades. Create an independent, FTC-backed certification that measures delivered effective GB on standard workload traces, so OEMs can sell and procurement can count 'certified 1.6x effective memory' with smaller physical DRAM.
why: Demand-side supply: if buyers trust 1.5-2x compressed capacity, DRAM content per laptop/phone/server can drop 25-40% during the shortage.

title: Rotational molding: scramble stashed activations so flips average to zero
idea: Rotomolding spins the mold on two axes so material deposits evenly, with no bias. DRAM retention failures are one-directional (charged cells lose charge), which biases the value errors. Activations saved for backprop are therefore stored at 4 bits in 1%-BER cells, XORed with a PRNG mask whose per-block seed lets the mask be regenerated on read. A charge-loss flip then means +2^k or -2^k with equal probability, so the noise is zero-mean and gradients stay unbiased, only slightly noisier than SGD already is.
why: The activation stash is the largest training memory consumer; an unprotected 4-bit stash cuts it about 4x and moves it to cheap cells without checkpoint recompute.
note: XOR mask turns one-way leakage flips into zero-mean noise; neat, cheap to prove.

title: Erasure-flagging sense amps: weak decisions marked, not guessed
idea: Limit: accept a raw bit error rate of 1e-4. A second, time-delayed sample in each SA flags bits that resolved slowly (small |dV|) as erasures, and a short per-burst erasure code corrects up to 4 flagged bits per 64 B with little overhead, since known-location errors cost half the parity.
why: Sense margin: tolerating 1e-4 lets Cs shrink ~30% or refresh intervals lengthen 2-4x (facts 1, 3), with soft information borrowed from NAND applied to DRAM.
note: Slow-resolving SA bits flagged as erasures double what ECC can correct; this is NAND soft info applied to DRAM.

title: Hadamard-spread embedding storage turns bit flips into faint Gaussian noise
idea: Shift the unit of meaning from bits to whole vectors: embeddings are stored after a fixed Hadamard rotation and spread-spectrum quantization, so any 1% of flipped bits perturb every coordinate slightly instead of wrecking a few; the inverse transform runs in the near-memory logic die as data streams out.
why: Lets the largest AI capacity consumers (recommendation tables, retrieval indexes, KV caches) live in no-ECC 1%-BER memory with negligible accuracy loss, ~2x lower cost per usable bit.
note: Spreading equalizes but does not shrink MSB-flip error energy; value depends on cheap high-BER DRAM existing.

title: Utility meters, not itemized bills: fixed-size recurrent state in SRAM
idea: Borrowed from utility meters that keep a running total instead of every transaction: most attention layers are replaced by fixed-size recurrent/state-space states (a few MB per sequence) held in SRAM, plus a few exact-attention layers over a short local window.
why: Removes the linearly growing KV cache from DRAM; per-sequence memory becomes constant and fits on-die, so refresh power is zero.
note: Removes growing KV; known hybrids (Jamba, Samba); long-range recall without global attention is the doubt.

title: Recompute-as-correction for KV caches and activations
idea: Ideal: memory errors are free to fix because the data can be regenerated. Closest: AI KV-cache and activation buffers are stored in unprotected relaxed-refresh DRAM with only a 16-bit CRC per 1 KB block; on a CRC miss the runtime recomputes that block from upstream tokens or layers instead of correcting it.
why: Facts 3 and 5: removes ECC storage and most refresh for the largest AI memory consumer; recompute costs <0.1% of FLOPs at 1e-7 block error rates.
note: CRC plus regeneration replaces ECC for KV/activations; easy software demo.

title: Expire-and-regenerate pages: let cells decay, recompute on miss
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: disable refresh entirely; each DRAM page carries a write timestamp, and any page older than its guaranteed retention counts as discarded, so reading it traps to the runtime, which regenerates the data from source (re-decompress weights from flash, recompute activations from checkpoints, refetch KV from a cheaper tier).
why: Zero refresh power; because regeneration is rare for hot data, the fab can target ~10 ms retention instead of 64 ms, cutting required Cs ~3x and with it capacitor height, etch time and support masks (facts 1, 3, 4).

title: Minify resident chat sessions with typing-indicator KV prefetch
idea: Minify how long an LLM session's KV cache stays in HBM/DRAM: idle sessions are parked compressed in CXL flash. A restore is triggered by early client signals (tab focus, the typing indicator, a cursor in the input box), so the ~1-3 s it takes a human to type hides the reload.
why: Most conversations sit idle >90% of wall-clock time, so the resident KV footprint drops ~3-5x with no added latency the user can see.

title: Bit-plane segmented KV cache with attention-gated plane residency
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: split every FP16 KV vector into a high plane (sign, exponent, top mantissa bits) and a low-mantissa plane stored in separate pages; only high planes stay in HBM, low planes live in CXL/LPDDR or NVMe and are fetched only for tokens whose coarse attention score (computed from high planes alone) lands in the top-k. Resolves 'keep all context' vs 'keep little memory' by holding every token coarsely and few tokens fully, losslessly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context serving memory; ~2-3x less HBM per session with a lossless fallback, so fewer HBM stacks (HBM TSV tax, cost/bit).
note: Coarse high planes for scoring plus lossless low-plane fetch for top-k; limited to ~2x.

title: JPEG for the KV cache: DCT along the token axis
idea: Treat each attention head's K and V as an image (tokens x channels), apply a block DCT along the token axis where neighbouring tokens correlate, and quantize with per-head learned quantization tables like JPEG luminance tables; the attention kernel inverse-transforms blocks in SRAM.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory; transform coding before quantization claims 4-8x smaller KV at <1% quality loss vs ~2-4x for plain quantization.

title: Bicycle gears: bit-plane tiering serves weights at shiftable precision
idea: Store weights transposed into bit-planes: the 4 most-significant planes stay in DRAM/HBM, low planes live in CXL or flash; each request 'shifts gear' by fetching only as many planes as its quality tier needs, and speculative decoding uses MSB-only planes as a free draft model.
why: Cuts DRAM held for weights 2-4x without storing multiple quantized copies; fetch energy scales with precision actually used.

title: Temporal mipmap KV cache with on-demand full-resolution recall
idea: Attention K/V is stored as a pyramid over token time. The last ~2k tokens stay at full resolution. Older spans are pooled into 8- and 64-token summary vectors that stay in HBM, while their full-resolution copies are parked in flash. When a query puts more than a threshold of attention mass on a summary, the controller fetches that span at full resolution for the next step, like texture mipmapping applied to time.
why: Resident KV grows roughly logarithmically instead of linearly with context, needing 5-10x less HBM at 128k-1M tokens while the detail that is needed can still be recalled.

title: Phylogenetic tree storage for resident model variants
idea: All fine-tuned variants resident on a node form an evolutionary tree. Each node stores 1-bit sign deltas plus per-channel scales relative to its parent, rebuilt on the fly in the GEMM epilogue. Serving 100 variants costs about one base model plus 100 x 1/16 of its size.
why: Multi-tenant serving memory falls 10-30x compared with separate copies. This extends LoRA-style sharing to full fine-tunes.
note: BitDelta-style 1-bit deltas arranged hierarchically; easy software demo.

title: Sodium spikes: streaming transformers store only the KV that fires
idea: Like a neuron's Na+ action potential that fires only past threshold, a video/audio streaming model compares each new frame's token KV with the co-located token of the previous frame and stores a new entry only if the change exceeds a learned per-layer threshold; unchanged tokens become 2-byte back-references.
why: Static-camera, screen and speech streams repeat 70-95% of tokens frame to frame; KV for long streaming contexts shrinks 5-20x (density, cost/bit).
note: Temporal token reduction for video LLMs is an active area; per-layer thresholding a twist.

title: Molybdenite exfoliation: peel only the bit-planes a token needs
idea: MoS2 peels into single layers; weights are stored bit-plane-major in row-aligned tiles (all MSBs of a tile together, then the next bit), and a per-token difficulty predictor fetches 2, 3, 4 or 8 planes, so easy tokens run a lower-precision model from the same single copy without overfetching unused planes.
why: Fetching 2-3 planes for most decode steps instead of 16-bit weights cuts weight bits moved ~6-8x on average and >10x on easy tokens, and LSB planes of cold layers can be evicted to flash (energy, density).

title: Batch blender: Hadamard-mix tensors so bit flips become diffuse noise
idea: Bulk blenders homogenize a batch so that no pocket is off-spec. Tensors are multiplied by a randomized Hadamard transform before quantization and storage, so after the fast inverse transform in the load path, one flipped value is spread at low amplitude across 256-4096 reconstructed values. The same rotation flattens outliers, which allows 3-4-bit quantization.
why: Sparse catastrophic errors become Gaussian-like noise about 1/sqrt(N) in amplitude, so 1%-BER storage costs only a small SNR penalty while the data is also quantized 4x.
note: Hadamard rotation (QuaRot-style) doubles as error spreading, letting high-BER relaxed-refresh storage carry quantized tensors.

title: Return-time-predicted KV hibernation for idle chat sessions
idea: Imposed limit: an idle conversation may hold zero KV bytes in DRAM. When a user goes idle, the KV cache is dropped and only token IDs are kept; a predictor that reads typing indicators, tab focus and the user's past think-times schedules a re-prefill on spare compute a few seconds before the next message is expected.
why: Idle sessions hold a large share of KV memory in chat serving; trading cheap compute for scarce DRAM can cut resident KV 3-10x, with sub-second latency cost when the prediction is right.
note: Return-time prediction adds to known KV drop-and-recompute; re-prefill compute cost is real at long context.

title: Bit-exact integer reversible transformers erase the activation stash
idea: Imposed limit: training may store activations for only one layer. Residual blocks use invertible coupling and run in fixed-point integer arithmetic, so the backward pass rebuilds each layer's input exactly, with no floating-point drift, and no activation stack is stored.
why: Activations dominate training memory at long sequence lengths; making activation memory independent of depth cuts training DRAM/HBM 3-10x for about 1.3-1.5x more compute.

title: Band-offset quantum-well bits stacked along a superlattice pillar
idea: Worse: store each bit on a bulky capacitor needing femtofarads. Flip: etch vertical pillars through a Si/Ge-rich superlattice, wrap each Ge-rich well with a tier gate, and store holes in its valence-band well (up to ~0.5 eV offset) as the bit, sensed as a threshold shift of the shared vertical Si channel, which is capacitorless and has no oxide tunneling, so endurance stays unlimited.
why: Every tier of every pillar is a bit: 128 tiers at 50 nm pillar pitch is ~17 nm2/bit (~50x), so 10x survives even at 20% array efficiency with NAND-like process cost; retention from thermal emission over the band offset is the speculative part.
note: Capacitorless bit per tier gives ~50x density; doubt: 0.5 eV offset means ~us retention at 85C, not ms.

title: Capacitor-hole racetrack: electroplated domain-wall nanowires in DRAM's high-aspect-ratio mold
idea: Etch the standard honeycomb hole lattice (~20 nm diameter at 35-40 nm pitch) in oxide. Instead of conformal ALD electrodes, electroplate a magnetic nanowire up from a seed at the hole bottom, modulating composition (Co-rich/Ni-rich, or thin Cu spacers) every ~60 nm to make pinning notches. Bits are axial domains separated by Bloch-point domain walls, which cylindrical wires carry without the Walker breakdown that slows flat racetracks. A vertical select transistor under each hole (4F2/6F2 vertical-channel style) drives ~30 uA bipolar shift pulses through the wire. A 20 nm MTJ on the planarised top reads the top bit and writes it (STT, or SOT from a top heavy-metal line). Half of each track is shift buffer, giving 10 data bits per 1.3 um hole and 25 per 3 um hole.
why: ~10x (1.3 um holes) to ~25x (3 um holes) bits per 1-beta cell footprint: 4.5-11 Gb/mm2 in principle, or 1-beta density at ~3x larger F with no EUV. Refresh energy goes to zero.
note: 10-25 bits per capacitor hole; doubts: notch electroplating in 20 nm AR-65 holes, shift reliability and heating at ~1e7 A/cm2.

title: Octopus arm ganglia: in-tier decoders built in the same channel film
idea: Octopus arms carry their own ganglia; in a 3D stack, form a small oxide-TFT decoder in each tier from the same channel film and the same slit/hole patterning as the cells, so each tier needs only ~log2(N) shared address lines instead of N individually contacted wordlines.
why: Per-tier contacts, staircases and CMOS drivers stop growing with tier count, so 120+ tiers (~10x bits/mm2) can be built without the periphery (49% of the die) and contact cost scaling up (facts 2, 7).
note: Shared-film decoders per tier cut wordline contacts to log2(N); doubt: decoder TFT quality from lateral cell patterning.

title: Automata Processor fixed: one hard-wired in-DRAM job, KV-cache top-k filtering
idea: Micron's Automata Processor died because nobody wanted to program NFAs and DRAM-process logic was slow. Hard-wire one function with a huge market: each bank's sense-amp stripe computes 4-bit dot products of a broadcast query against the open row of keys and returns only the indices of the top-k matches, so the accelerator fetches just those KV entries through one new command and no programming model.
why: Overfetch and data movement (facts 5, 8): long-context attention moves 10-30x less KV data off-chip, using bank-level parallelism for TB/s internal bandwidth.
note: Bank-level top-k cuts long-context KV traffic 10-30x; area in the sense-amp stripe and approximate-attention accuracy are doubts.

title: Top-k memory: base die filters KV cache before the link
idea: Invert 'memory returns what was asked for': for attention, the host sends the query vector to the HBM base die, which scores keys in low precision across the KV pages beneath it and returns only the top-k keys/values at full precision.
why: Long-context decode is KV-bandwidth-bound; returning 5-10% of KV entries cuts link traffic 10-20x and lets longer contexts live in fewer, cheaper stacks.
note: 10-20x less KV link traffic in long-context decode; doubt: low-precision top-k accuracy, and attention-PIM is crowded art.

title: Mycorrhizal memory sharing: gradient-driven DRAM lending between servers
idea: Servers on a CXL switch fabric run a decentralized 'wood-wide-web' protocol: each node advertises a scalar gradient (free memory minus pressure), and pages flow one hop at a time from surplus to starved neighbours, the way mycorrhizal fungi move sugar from sunlit to shaded trees. There is no global allocator; borrowed pages carry a lease that is recalled when the donor's gradient flips.
why: Usable supply: datacenters strand ~20-30% of installed DRAM; reclaiming half of it equals ~10-15% more effective DRAM supply with zero new wafers.
note: Decentralized gradient diffusion of pages; pooling itself widely pursued.

title: Diversified-portfolio DIMMs mixing vendors inside each codeword
idea: Portfolio theory cuts risk by holding uncorrelated assets. Build ECC modules in which the chips of each codeword come from 2-3 vendors or process lots. Systematic weaknesses (TRR bypass patterns, temperature-dependent retention) then stay uncorrelated, and chipkill absorbs one vendor's failure mode. Module design, qualification and a pilot run fit in $1M.
why: Makes cheaper second-source dies, including new or U.S. entrants, usable at low risk. That diversifies supply and lowers cost per bit.
note: Decorrelates systematic failure modes under chipkill; mixed-vendor timing qualification is the work.

title: Open-PDK shuttle CMOS plus university BEOL cell post-processing
idea: Combine open-source SKY130/GF180 shuttle chips carrying sense amps, ECC and refresh controllers with university post-processing of capacitor or oxide-TFT arrays on the top-metal pads, giving full-stack reliability testbeds (real arrays plus real ECC) for a few tens of thousands of dollars. Buildable in a university nanofab: low-temperature BEOL steps on diced shuttle die.
why: Speeds iteration on reliability schemes for new cells (facts 2, 3) and builds US memory know-how; a strategy rather than a cell.

title: Chilled-DIMM certification grade with 256 ms refresh
idea: Worse: run DRAM at 85-95 C, where leakage doubles every ~10 C. Flip: create a 'cold-loop' grade: modules on datacenter liquid cold plates held at 25-35 C are binned and certified for 256 ms refresh, and dies that fail the hot spec but pass cold are sold into this grade.
why: Fact 3 and yield: 4x less refresh and a new outlet for retention-weak dies that would otherwise be scrapped; rides on the liquid cooling already arriving with AI racks.

title: Eliminate test hardware: bootable signed DIMM health certificate
idea: Eliminate expensive ATE for used-memory trust: a free bootable image runs 8-hour retention, pattern and row-hammer tests on any host and signs the result with the module's SPD serial; ~$600k builds the software, signing service and three pilot broker integrations in 18 months.
why: Trust is the bottleneck in reuse; certified used DRAM sells at 40-60% of new and unlocks stranded DDR4 inventory.

title: Eliminate royalty fear: expired-patent freedom-to-operate atlas for legacy DRAM
idea: Eliminate the belief that DRAM is a legal minefield: a ~$400k legal-engineering project maps expired pre-2006 DRAM patents onto a complete 50-90nm stacked-capacitor process and periphery, publishing an open freedom-to-operate atlas and reference flow.
why: Cuts legal cost for any legacy-node entrant from millions to near zero, enabling US micro-fabs and foundries.

title: Eliminate shred-everything policy: volatile-memory sanitization clause
idea: Eliminate the security rule that sends decommissioned DRAM to shredders: a ~$300k study measures room-temperature data remanence after power-off and drives a 'power-cycled DRAM is sanitized' clause with a verification test into NIST SP 800-88 guidance and corporate disposal policies.
why: Many enterprises shred all memory by default; one policy change releases millions of DIMMs a year for reuse.
note: Cheap remanence study; NIST guidance may already treat power removal as sufficient.

title: Eliminate software bloat: memory-footprint bounties for top open-source apps
idea: Eliminate wasted bytes: a $1M bounty fund pays per verified MB saved, times installed base, for merged patches that cut resident memory in Chromium, Electron, Firefox, Kubernetes components and JVM defaults, measured on a public benchmark.
why: A 10% cut in browser/Electron memory across billions of devices frees hundreds of PB of effective capacity and delays RAM upgrades.

title: Eliminate lost know-how: retired DRAM engineers' knowledge guild
idea: Eliminate relearning lost US DRAM know-how: a ~$400k program records structured process-knowledge interviews with retired engineers from closed US and European DRAM fabs, builds a searchable knowledge base, and runs a paid advisory guild for new entrants.
why: Shortens new-entrant learning curves by years; tacit yield knowledge is the scarcest asset after capital.
note: Cheap and executable; tacit knowledge transfer is partial.

title: Librarian's catalog: signed lifetime passport on every DIMM
idea: Each module's SPD carries a signed lifetime log written by the host BMC: power-on hours, thermal history, corrected-error counts, row-hammer events. Second-hand buyers can grade modules the way a library tracks a book's condition, and a public registry prices reuse by verified health.
why: Reuse supply: buyers' distrust is the main barrier to secondary DRAM markets; verified provenance could lift reuse from <10% to 40%+ of retired server DRAM.
note: SMART-like logs for DIMMs; low-cost firmware pilot.

title: Open-hardware DRAM tester kits that issue signed grade certificates
idea: Learning from ham-radio networks, a 10-person company sells ~$300 FPGA tester kits with secure elements to e-waste recyclers worldwide. Each run produces a cryptographically signed certificate (pattern suite, retention, speed bin) bound to the module serial, so remote buyers can trust second-hand memory.
why: Trust is the bottleneck in secondary memory markets; signed provenance could unlock millions of modules a year.
note: Cheap signed-certificate testers address buyer distrust in used memory.

title: DRAM as lossy mirror of flash: refetch instead of protect
idea: Reverse which copy is authoritative: for clean (read-mostly) pages such as model weights and file cache, a cheap checksum detects errors on reject-grade 1%-BER dies and the line is refetched from the SSD copy.
why: Lets low-grade dies serve large read-mostly footprints, adding usable capacity without new wafers.

title: Lunar-base abundant-element PDK: a gain cell from only eight elements
idea: A Moon-base fab could use only regolith-abundant elements, so impose that rule in a university nanofab: build a 2T gain-cell array from Si, O, N, Al, Ti and H (plus B/P dopants) only, with poly-Si channels, LPCVD SiO2/Si3N4, ALD Al2O3, sputtered Al and TiN, and contact lithography on 100 mm wafers. Benchmark retention against a W/ZrO2 reference.
why: Proves a chokepoint-free memory process (no W, Hf, Zr, Ta, Co, In or Ga) and gives a template for a resource-proof U.S. DRAM tier.
note: Essentially a 1970s poly-Si gain-cell process; easy demo, low step change.

title: Pinned-photodiode buried node borrowed from image-sensor foundries
idea: MAGNIFY retention by holding the bit in a fully depleted, surface-pinned buried n-well (a CIS pinned photodiode kept dark, dark current ~1-10 e-/s) with a transfer gate and source-follower readout like a global-shutter pixel memory, taped out on a commercial CIS MPW.
why: Retention of seconds to minutes at ~2,000 e- cuts refresh energy and bandwidth >100x (fact 3) on a known foundry process; ~0.5-1 um2 cells suit low-power embedded tiers.
note: CIS pinned node gives long retention on a known process; large cells, niche.

title: Two-hundred-variant bit-cell zoo on every shuttle run
idea: MAGNIFY variants and MINIFY cost per experiment: tile 200 bit-cell variants (gain cells, varactor caps, bootstrapped switches, leakage latches) with on-die retention/endurance BIST on each $10-20k MPW shuttle, publish an open retention-tail database and license the winners.
why: Cuts cell-discovery cycles from years to quarters and feeds U.S. fabs with characterized cells (facts 3, 4).
note: Cheap MPW characterization; incremental discovery value.

title: Open-source DRAM-cell library on US foundry PDKs
idea: Worsen: keep storage-cell know-how locked inside three companies. Flip: spend $1M over 24 months designing, taping out and publishing open-source eDRAM and gain cells (thick-oxide 3T, MIM 1T1C) on SkyWater 130 and 22FDX PDKs with measured retention data, so any US chip team can add dense memory.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply diversification; lowers the entry cost for new memory makers.
note: Clearly executable on open PDKs; ecosystem value, not a step change in cost per bit.

title: Sell retention-fallout dies as permanent fast-refresh DDR5 SKUs
idea: Forced limit (DDR/HBM interface unchanged): standard controllers only. Dies that miss 64 ms retention because of a weak-cell tail are fused to always report the hot-temperature refresh-rate code (2x or 4x refresh) in the existing MR4 register, so stock controllers refresh them faster, and they sell at a discount into capacity-hungry, bandwidth-tolerant tiers such as CXL expanders and inference KV-cache.
why: Recovers a few percent of wafer output now scrapped or downbinned, raising usable bit supply immediately with zero capex (cost per bit, supply).
note: Uses existing MR4 refresh-rate code; modest supply gain.

title: Moth-ear minimal-periphery eDRAM compiler for open U.S. PDKs
idea: Noctuid moths detect bats with ears of just two neurons. An open-source compiler for SkyWater 130/GF180 generates 3T gain-cell eDRAM macros with radically minimal periphery: single-ended inverter sensing, shared counter refresh and standard-cell decoders. Two shuttles validate it for ~$700k in 24 months.
why: U.S. manufacturability: gives domestic mature-node fabs a working-memory macro ~2-3x denser than SRAM for chiplets now, seeding a U.S. DRAM design base.
note: Open gain-cell eDRAM compiler on U.S. PDKs; academic precedents exist.

title: Magnify contributors: open-source 3D DRAM compiler and PDK
idea: Fund three engineers to release an open-source array generator for SKY130 and GF180, plus a parametric 3D DRAM tier model (tier count, Cs, leakage tail, spares) and a cost and yield calculator, so universities can tape out DRAM arrays on open shuttles.
why: U.S. manufacturability and talent: brings hundreds of designers to array architecture for about $900k.

title: Retention-DLTS fingerprints the defect species behind the leakage tail
idea: Treat a commodity DRAM as a billion-pixel deep-level transient spectrometer. Measure each weak cell's retention time against temperature (the Arrhenius slope gives trap energy) and against wordline/plate bias (the field-enhancement factor separates Poole-Frenkel, phonon-assisted tunneling and GIDL). Cluster the signatures across vendors and lots to name the dominant defect species (Fe-B, vacancy-oxygen, interface Pb centers).
why: Knowing which defect sets the 13 fA tail tells fabs which fix (gettering, passivation or field relief) buys the most refresh relief. A two-person lab with FPGA testers and thermal chambers can do it for <$500k in 18 months (fact 3).
note: Executable lab study; retention activation-energy studies exist, cross-vendor fingerprinting is the twist.

title: Retired hyperscale DIMMs re-certified with a per-module retention passport
idea: Second-hand DRAM has not won trust because buyers cannot see a module's wear or retention. A test cell measures each retired DIMM's retention tail at temperature and writes a module-specific refresh multiplier and a weak-row list into its SPD. Modules with leakier access transistors then run at 2x refresh instead of being scrapped.
why: Raises usable memory supply through recycling during a ~4x price spike, handling the leakage tail with per-module refresh instead of discard.

title: Cookie-cutter procedural data regenerated from seeds instead of stored
idea: Like stamping cookies from a cutter instead of storing them, replace stored tensors that are pseudo-random or structured (random projections, initializations, LoRA bases, positional tables, dropout masks) with seeds plus near-memory generators. These recreate each line at access time.
why: Zero refresh: data that is never stored never needs refresh. It also cuts the DRAM footprint and data-movement energy (fact 5) for that share of memory.

title: Thousand tiny tapeouts: crowdsourced access-device leakage variants on open PDKs
idea: 10-person constraint: crowdsource the search a small team cannot fund. Publish an open eDRAM access-device test-cell template for open-PDK shuttles (SKY130, GF180, IHP SG13G2). Pay bounties to hobbyists and students whose variants (gate shapes, well-bias tricks, guard rings, stacked devices) beat the baseline in silicon-measured retention, ranked by an automated FPGA tester.
why: Fact 3: hundreds of cheap parallel experiments explore leakage geometry faster than one team could, and the winners feed tail-reduction techniques into licensable IP.
note: Open-PDK 130-180 nm leakage physics transfers poorly to DRAM access devices.

title: Generated embeddings: replace terabyte tables with tiny hash-fed networks
idea: Po: the table is stored inside a brain. Recommender embedding tables are replaced by a multi-hash encoder feeding a small MLP that generates each ID's embedding on the fly, with only the hottest ~1% of IDs cached explicitly.
why: Embedding tables are TB-scale DRAM hogs in recommendation; generation cuts them 10-100x at modest compute cost.
note: Recsys is the largest DRAM user; DHE-style generation known, compute and accuracy tradeoff is the doubt.

title: Swap fixed GC heap sizing for cluster memory-price-driven heaps
idea: Substitute DRAM headroom with CPU cycles when DRAM is dear. The scheduler publishes a live per-GB memory price, and the JVM, Go, .NET and V8 runtimes read it to retune their heap targets: they collect more often and return pages when memory is expensive and grow when it is cheap. Unchanged hardware.
why: Managed runtimes keep 1.5-3x the live set as headroom. Price-driven sizing reclaims 20-40% of managed-heap DRAM fleet-wide for a few percent of CPU.

title: Export idle host DRAM of GPU servers as far memory
idea: Inverts 'a server's DRAM serves only its own CPU': GPU servers carry 1-2 TB of host DRAM that sits mostly idle while the GPUs work from HBM. An RDMA far-memory daemon leases those idle bytes to neighboring CPU servers for swap and tiering over existing NICs.
why: Unlocks 30-60% of host DRAM in AI racks for the rest of the fleet with no new chips.

title: Dictionary: fleet-trained compression dictionaries pinned per workload
idea: Train zstd-style dictionaries per workload class (JVM heaps, Python objects, embeddings) from fleet samples, ship them signed with the binary, and pin them in the hardware compressor's SRAM so even single 4 KB pages compress against a rich shared context.
why: Small-page ratio rises from ~2x to 3x or more, making zswap/hardware compressed tiers 30-50% more effective at saving DRAM.

title: Run cache-sized services on gigabyte-LLC CPUs with minimal DIMMs
idea: Box: substitute × existing large-L3 CPUs (~1 GB stacked SRAM) × whole working set × deployment time × minimal DIMM population. Routers, rate limiters, feature-flag and session services whose working sets fit in ~1 GB are pinned to large-cache parts already in the fleet, with one small DIMM per channel.
why: Those services get 256–512 GB per box by default; running them cache-resident frees 80–95% of their DRAM using installed silicon, so nothing new passes through fluorinated etch or PFAS lithography.

title: Seed-bank keeper: pages stored as generator plus seed
idea: A seed bank stores seeds, not forests. A userfaultfd library lets programs register regions produced by deterministic generators (PRNG noise, dropout masks, random projections, synthetic test data, procedurally initialized tensors) as (generator ID, seed, offset). Under pressure the pages are dropped, and on a fault they are regenerated bit-exactly with vectorized Philox at >10 GB/s.
why: Random data defeats every compressor yet has near-zero Kolmogorov size. This frees tens of GB per training or simulation node for about $300k of engineering.
note: Small real footprint; frameworks already regenerate dropout masks from seeds.

title: Monk with one bowl: eBPF census finds duplicate buffer copies
idea: A monk owns one bowl, not five. An eBPF plus page-hash census tool samples contents across the page cache, socket buffers, user heaps and GPU staging buffers and flags identical data held in two or more places (the NIC-kernel-user-serialize-GPU chain). The team then ships upstream zero-copy patches (io_uring registered buffers, splice, mmap'd page cache) for the top offenders.
why: Data-path services hold 2-5 copies of in-flight data. A small team can free 10-25% of DRAM on storage, proxy and ingest nodes.

title: Soviet-style socialist competition: bounties for memory-footprint patches
idea: Like a five-year-plan competition, but paid. A $600k bounty pool pays per verified GB saved on standard benchmarks of the 50 most-deployed open-source infrastructure packages (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch, PyTorch DataLoader, Chromium). A $400k CI harness measures peak and steady RSS before and after each merged patch.
why: Code that runs on millions of servers multiplies every saving: a 10% footprint cut in these packages frees millions of GB globally, which may be the highest-leverage use of $1M.

title: Carbon backbone documents: schema skeleton shared, only functional groups stored
idea: Organic molecules share a carbon backbone and differ only in functional groups; an in-memory document store (JSON/protobuf caches, Redis hashes) hash-conses each distinct key-set and type layout once as a backbone, and stores each document as a backbone ID plus a packed value vector, with a shape-lookup instruction so a field access stays one dependent load.
why: Repeated keys, type tags and padding are 40-70% of bytes in JSON-heavy caches; sharing backbones cuts those caches 2-3x in DRAM (cost/bit, density).

title: Fan-deck ordering: codebook indices where one flip yields a similar shade
idea: Paint fan decks put similar shades on adjacent cards, so grabbing the wrong one still looks right. For vector-quantized weights and embeddings, codebook indices are assigned by simulated annealing so that codewords whose indices differ by one bit are nearest neighbors in vector space (a Gray-like assignment). Indices are stored raw in 1%-BER cells, and a flip swaps in a nearly identical codeword.
why: Makes 2-3 bit/weight VQ (5-8x smaller than FP16) tolerant of 1% raw BER with no ECC; the assignment cuts flip distortion about 5-10x versus random index order.
note: Pseudo-Gray index assignment (channel-optimized VQ) applied to weights in faulty memory.

title: Swap layer-by-layer 3D stacking for rolling one patterned membrane
idea: Pattern one planar layer of thin-film gain cells with DUV on a strained SiNx bilayer, release it, and let the built-in strain roll it into a 20-winding tube. Each winding becomes a memory tier, and the tiers connect through edge contacts along the roll axis.
why: Gives 20 tiers from one deposition and patterning sequence (fact 2), so cost does not grow with the tier count, and no EUV is used (fact 4).
note: 20 tiers from one patterning would collapse 3D cost; dense edge interconnect across windings and alignment are the doubt.

title: Multilayer optical-disc focus addressing via threshold-coded tiers
idea: Like BD-XL picking a layer by focus depth, give each of 32 storage tiers on one shared vertical wordline a distinct access threshold set by deposited channel thickness; address tier k by stepping wordline voltage and differencing successive bitline reads, and write each column in descending-threshold order.
why: 10x at same cost: removes per-tier bitline staircases and select lines, so 32 tiers cost about one hole etch plus depositions; ~15x bits per footprint.
note: Addresses 32 tiers by Vt stepping, no staircases; doubt: Vt variation and read margin across 32 levels on one wordline.

title: Snack-bag web metallizers vacuum-coat 128-tier stacks by the kilometer
idea: Borrowed from roll-to-roll metallizers that coat packaging film at ~1,000 m/min: deposit 128 alternating Mo/SiOx wordline/insulator layers on a heat-tolerant web in multi-drum passes, laminate the stack onto a CMOS wafer, then one hole etch plus ALD finishes vertical-channel gain cells.
why: Tier-stack deposition is a dominant 3D cost; web coating is ~100x cheaper per m2, and with one mask for all tiers the path reaches ~$0.1/GB; trade-offs: lamination voids, lower tier quality, refresh-heavy cells.
note: Web-coated tier stacks could slash deposition cost; pinholes, lamination voids and etching through a web are the doubts.

title: Fifty-electron bit read by repeated non-destructive skipper sampling
