idea: MINIFY the stored charge ~600x (from ~30,000 e- to ~50 e-): the storage node is a ~0.01 fF floating diffusion with no capacitor, and a per-subarray skipper-CCD-style floating-gate amplifier shuttles the packet under its sense gate N=16 times, averaging read noise below 1 e- rms before write-back.
why: Deletes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the AR 60-75:1 etch; cell heads toward 4F2 and write CV2 energy falls ~100x. Only viable if node leakage is pushed to ~1e-21 A (pair with a wide-gap or pinned node).
note: ~600x less charge kills the capacitor wall; doubts: 1e-21 A node leakage and 16 skipper samples within DRAM latency.

title: Magnify the draw ratio: fiber-drawn lithography-free memory arrays
idea: Build a centimeter-scale preform holding thousands of channels of semiconductor glass, metal and insulator, thermally draw it 10,000:1 into km fibers so features shrink to sub-micron, then fuse and slice fiber bundles into faceplates where each core is a vertical transistor-capacitor cell addressed by one coarse metallization.
why: Drawing replaces lithography: one draw tower outputs km/hour, so array cost falls to ~cents/cm2, targeting ~100x lower $/GB for slow first-generation DRAM-like tiers.
note: Thermal drawing replaces litho cheaply; doubt: drawn semiconductors make poor transistors and per-bit density may lag badly.

title: Magnify throughput 100x: solar-style inline memory lines
idea: Borrow photovoltaic manufacturing (belt-fed inline PECVD, laser scribing, screen-print metallization at ~8,000 wafers/hour per line) to make vertical thin-film transistor-capacitor cells whose critical dimensions are set by film thickness and laser scribe, not lithography.
why: PV processes a wafer for ~$0.2 vs ~$5,000+ for DRAM; even holding ~1/500 of the bits, cost per GB drops ~100x+, accepting low density, big modules and slower first versions.
note: Key doubt: ~500x lower density makes modules huge; periphery and RC still need fine litho.

title: Minify reliability to 1e-3 BER: junk-tolerant stacked memory
idea: Sell memory for noise-tolerant AI tensors at a raw 1e-3 bit error rate: skip sort, burn-in, repair and final test, let each die self-map defects via boot-time BIST, and absorb errors with stochastic rounding and error-resilient training.
why: Dropping the yield gate lets fabs stack 64 cheap thin-film cell layers whose compound yield would otherwise be near zero, and removes ~25-40% test/repair cost; together these target ~100x lower $/GB.
note: Error tolerance unlocks low-yield 64-tier stacks; doubt: 1e-3 raw BER corrupts exponent bits unless critical bits get protection.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: DRAM on Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build 12-16 tiers of oxide-TFT gain cells at F~0.5 um on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in under-used LCD/OLED fabs, which already own panel-scale litho, sputter and PECVD. One panel has ~60x the area of a 300 mm wafer, so even at coarse F it holds ~3-7 TB of capacity-tier memory behind a CXL-style controller.
why: Capital and crucible chokepoint: display-fab capex per m2 is ~50-100x lower than a DRAM fab, with no Czochralski silicon, quartz crucible or EUV; targets ~$1-3/GB for a slower (~100 ns) tier that frees real DRAM for hot data.
note: Idle Gen-8.5 LCD fabs as capacity-tier memory; doubt: 12-16 tier panel yield and defect density at panel scale.

title: Vacuum as the insulator: field-emission two-terminal crossbar storage cell
idea: Reverse insulator and conductor: each storage node is a metal island over a sealed 3-5 nm vacuum gap to a sharp emitter at a wordline/bitline crossing; below the Fowler-Nordheim threshold the gap passes essentially nothing, while ~2x the field drives uA emission to charge or discharge it in ns.
why: Leakage tail and 3D blocker (facts 2,3): super-exponential I-V gives >1e12 on/off with no transistor, so 4F2 crossbar tiers can stack with no lateral transistor at all.
note: Super-exponential FN I-V as built-in selector; doubt: sealed 3-5 nm gaps, emitter wear, and tiny island charge readout.

title: Roll a 2D array film into a multi-turn scroll
idea: Turn area into tiers by rolling instead of stacking: fabricate a thin-film oxide DRAM array on a strained bilayer membrane with the existing mask set, then use one added release mask so the film self-rolls into a 10-30 turn Swiss roll, with turns connected through contacts at the scroll edge.
why: Density and 3D cost (facts 2,4): 10-30x bits per footprint without per-tier processing; rolled-up nanomembrane capacitors already exist.
note: 10-30 tiers from one patterned film; doubt: connecting inner turns and yield of rolled arrays.

title: Another dimension: 512-tier vertical charge-coupled strings with one sense node
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bits are charge packets in potential wells along a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel gated by 512 stacked wordline plates, a one-hole 3D-NAND-like process with no capacitor and no per-bit transistor. Reads clock the packets CCD-style down the pillar into one floating-diffusion sense node under the array, which regenerates them and re-injects them at the top, so refresh is just recirculation.
why: 100x path: NAND-like cost (~$0.05-0.15/GB) because periphery is one sense node per 512 bits, no EUV and few masks per tier; trade-offs: serial 10-50 us page access, and charge-transfer inefficiency and dark current cap string length, so a small DRAM cache must front it. Attacks Facts 1, 2, 4 and 7.
note: NAND-like cost for refresh-by-recirculation memory; but 10-50 us serial access is not DRAM-class, and CTI over 512 transfers is doubtful.

title: Blessing in disguise: Geiger-mode avalanche bitline sensing of 100-electron cells
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise turns breakdown, normally a failure, into gain: each bitline segment ends in a SPAD-like junction biased just above avalanche breakdown, which a stored packet of ~100 electrons triggers into a full-swing self-quenched pulse, so storage nodes need only ~0.02 fF and can be plain planar diffusions.
why: 100x path: deletes the capacitor module (Fact 1) and allows near-4F2 planar or stacked cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: dark counts and afterpulsing need repeat reads and strong ECC, ~10-100 ns quench recovery and higher sense voltage. Attacks Facts 1, 2 and 4.
note: Avalanche gain could delete the capacitor module; doubts are dark counts, afterpulsing, high bias at DRAM pitch, junction leakage swamping 100-electron packets.

title: Coaxial gallium-oxide 2T0C cell grown inside one vertical hole
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: in a 3D-NAND-like stack of word planes, one DUV-printed hole receives nested ALD shells at each tier recess - an outer amorphous Ga2O3 write channel gated by the plane, a metal storage-node ring, a thin dielectric, and an inner Ga2O3 read channel gated by that ring.
why: Ga2O3's 4.8 eV gap gives off-current below ~1e-21 A, so retention exceeds years and refresh is zero with no capacitor module; one hole mask serves 32-64 tiers, raising density without EUV (facts 2, 3, 4).
note: Refresh-free multi-tier gain cell from one hole; ALD amorphous Ga2O3 mobility and nested-shell control are the doubt.

title: Pollen-tube confined epitaxy grows monocrystalline channels in every tier
idea: A pollen tube grows only inside the style's channel; deposit a cheap 120-pair PECVD oxide/nitride stack as in 3D NAND, strip the nitride through slits to leave tunnels, then grow single-crystal Si into all tunnels at once by template-confined lateral epitaxy seeded from the substrate at each slit base.
why: Replaces slow, strain-limited Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattices (capped near 30-60 layers) with 3D-NAND-cost stacks, making 120 tiers (~10x bits/mm2) affordable at near-flat wafer cost (fact 2).
note: Single-crystal Si grown into NAND-style nitride-strip tunnels; lateral confined-epi distance and defects are the doubt.

title: Apical-meristem nanowires grow stacked transistors along their own axis
idea: Shoots add segments at the tip; grow vertical Si nanowires by catalyst-tip (VLS) growth from the pad lattice while switching dopant and Ge gases every ~25 nm, so each wire holds 16 axial n+/p/n+ transistor segments, then fill around the forest with alternating spin-on dielectric and conductor layers that become wordline tiers timed to the segments.
why: Channels for all 16 tiers come from one growth run instead of patterning; at ~40 nm wire pitch that is ~100 nm2 per bit, ~8-10x bits/mm2 at roughly flat cost (fact 2).
note: All tiers' channels from one VLS growth; aligning wordline tiers to dopant segments and catalyst contamination are the doubt.

title: Myelin multilamellar self-assembly lays down twenty tiers in one coat
idea: Schwann cells wrap axons in dozens of uniform lamellae; spin a high-chi lamellar block copolymer that orders parallel to the substrate into 20+ layers (~12 nm period), then use sequential infiltration synthesis to turn one block into AlOx insulator and the other into In2O3 channel, creating a whole tier stack in one coat-anneal-infiltrate sequence below 200 C.
why: Tier-stack cost drops from ~100 depositions to one coat plus a few infiltration cycles; 40+ BEOL-compatible tiers with a single hole/slit patterning give ~10x bits/mm2 at near-flat cost (facts 2, 4).
note: 40 tiers from one coat; SIS oxides are device-poor, and 12 nm period leaves no room for wordlines.

title: Cochlear amplifier: Hopf-poised sense amp hears sub-femtofarad cells
idea: Cochlear hair cells sit at a Hopf bifurcation, giving huge gain for faint sounds; bias each sense amplifier at the edge of oscillation with a calibrated negative-resistance loop so the tiny bitline perturbation of a ~1 fF cell tips it decisively, with per-amp calibration of the bifurcation point.
why: Capacitor charge wall: if 1-2 fF cells become readable, pillar AR can fall from 60-75:1 to ~15-20:1, cutting deposition/etch cost and opening lateral 3D capacitors.
note: Latches already regenerate from instability; Hopf poise does not beat kT/C noise or offset.

title: Airport baggage conveyor: vertical charge-coupled bit strings in 3D stacks
idea: Like bags riding a conveyor to one scanner, deposit a 3D-NAND-style stack of 64-128 gate layers around a vertical wide-gap channel (e.g., Ga2O3 or ZnSnO) and clock charge packets up and down it CCD-style; a single sense/restore node at the top of each string reads and rewrites packets as they pass. A bit is a potential well under a gate, so each tier costs one deposition, not a transistor plus capacitor.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 3D density without a 3D capacitor or lateral transistor; ~100 tiers at 3 gates/bit gives ~30 bits per hole, ~5-10x density with no added EUV; serial shift (~1 ns/stage) keeps average latency ~20-30 ns only if strings stay short.
note: Key doubt: charge-transfer efficiency in oxide channels over 100+ shifts; serial latency limits string length.

title: Photomultiplier read: avalanche gain junction under each pillar
idea: Like a photomultiplier or SPAD turning one photon into a pulse, place a quenched avalanche junction at the foot of each vertical bitline biased just below breakdown; a 0.1 fF cell's few hundred electrons trigger ~100x multiplication, then a passive quench resets it, so cells and lines stay tiny.
why: Capacitor wall and access energy (facts 1, 8): Cs drops ~50x and the local line stays a few fF; claims >10x lower energy per read if avalanche statistics and dark counts are tamed.
note: Avalanche gain lets Cs shrink ~50x; dark counts, gain noise and high bias fight the voltage floor.

title: Plated-wire memory rebuilt as vertical plated vias in 3D stacks
idea: Plated-wire memory (Voyager era) stored bits in the circumferential magnetization of permalloy plated on a wire and read them non-destructively by tilting it with a word strap. Make the wire a vertical copper pillar in a 3D-NAND-style hole lined with circumferentially anisotropic CoFeB, use the stacked tier planes as word straps, write by coincident pillar plus strap current, and read by a small strap pulse that tilts the film and induces a pillar voltage.
why: 100+ tiers from one hole etch with no lateral transistor or capacitor (Fact 2), non-destructive read (Fact 8), non-volatile (Fact 3); ~1/5 the cost per bit of 2D DRAM if signal suffices.
note: 100+ tiers from one hole etch; doubt: inductive read signal scales with flux area and is uV at nm scale.

title: Threshold-switch crossbar capacitors: 64 decks, refreshed constantly
idea: Inverts 'an access device must hold the bit for 64 ms': put a chalcogenide ovonic threshold switch in series with a tiny MIM capacitor at every crossbar node, stack 64 self-aligned decks with two KrF masks each, accept us-to-ms retention set by OTS leakage, and refresh whole decks in parallel from base CMOS.
why: 4F2 per deck with no transistor or EUV, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off is refresh power (~20-40% of total), half-select disturb and OTS drift.
note: us retention means ~1000x refresh rate; refresh power likely dominates, not 20-40%.

title: Memory that rots on purpose: nanoimprinted foil for short-lived data
idea: Inverts 'memory must keep data until overwritten': roll-to-roll nanoimprint (~100 nm) 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on metal foil with small leaky cells (1-10 ms retention, no refresh circuitry), laminate ~50 foils into a block, and let accelerators store only activations, gradients and KV pages consumed within the retention window, recomputing on rare loss.
why: Roll-to-roll layers cost ~$1-5/m2 versus ~$10,000/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so even at ~30x lower density it is ~100x cheaper per GB for transient data; trade-off: no long-term storage, ~100 ns-1 us access.
note: Ultra-cheap R2R layers for transient data; doubts: 100 nm R2R overlay, inter-foil interconnect, sub-µs access.

title: Self-assembled diode dots: block copolymers replace EUV for every cell
idea: Inverts 'lithography must define each access device': coat a PS-b-PDMS block copolymer guided by coarse 193 nm trenches into 10 nm-pitch dot arrays, then convert each dot by sequential infiltration synthesis into a vertical oxide Schottky diode atop a MIM nanocapacitor, mapping out defective dots at test.
why: Zero EUV layers (fact 4) and ~1 mask per tier at 10 nm pitch; with 8 tiers, ~100x lower cost per GB; trade-off is diode leakage forcing ms refresh and DSA defect remapping.
note: EUV-free 10 nm-pitch stacked tiers; doubts: DSA defectivity, SIS diode rectification, diode-access leakage.

title: Heat is the wordline: thermally gated access with 1.5 eV activation
idea: Inverts 'access devices are gated by voltage': put an ionic or deep-trap hopping conductor with ~1.5 eV activation energy in series with each capacitor, effectively insulating at 25 C (retention far beyond hours) while a nanosecond pulse in a row heater line takes it to ~400 C, raising conductance ~10^10x long enough to read or write; cells form 2-terminal crossbar stacks.
why: Two-terminal low-mask crossbar with refresh-free retention, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: heater energy per row access, thermal crosstalk, ~100 ns cycle.
note: 1.5 eV activation gives ~1e14 on/off between 25 and 400 C; doubts: heater energy, thermal crosstalk, dielectric leakage when hot.

title: One global clock restores every cell: gated-diode charge-pump bistables
idea: Inverts 'refresh is done row by row by sense amps': each cell is a gated diode (large capacitance when inverted, small when depleted) tied to a shared plate clock and a diode to the supply; a stored '1' couples the clock strongly and is topped up each cycle while a '0' couples weakly and stays below the diode threshold, so one global clock refreshes billions of cells at once.
why: Lets cheap leaky TFT or poly cells work with no row refresh, sense-amp refresh path or refresh controller (fact 7), ~2 devices per cell in low-mask tiers, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: continuous clock power and margin between stable points.
note: Global clock tops up only stored 1s, letting leaky TFT cells skip row refresh; doubt: continuous clock power and bistable margins across billions of cells.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche read of a hundred-electron storage node
idea: Shrink the storage node to ~20 aF holding ~100 electrons and wire it as the bias of a SPAD-like junction. At read the junction is armed above breakdown for ~2 ns: a stored '1' tips it into avalanche (gain ~1e5) and a '0' does not, then an active quench resets it.
why: Poisson statistics need only N >= 36 electrons for 6-sigma discrimination, and kT/C noise on 20 aF is ~2 electrons rms. Storing 31,000 electrons is an artifact of bitline charge sharing, so the capacitor shrinks ~50x, deleting the 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1) and 1-2 patterning layers (fact 4).
note: Shrinks storage node ~50x, but retention scales with C and avalanche dark counts/variability threaten read fidelity.

title: Partial-charge sip read makes DRAM sensing non-destructive
idea: A tightly controlled subthreshold wordline pulse lets only ~3% of the cell charge (~450 e-) leak into a 0.2 fF local sense node; kT/C charge noise there is ~6 e-, so 450 e- is a >20 sigma signal (~0.36 V). The cell keeps 97% of its charge, so nothing is restored and only the addressed 64 B is sensed; normal refresh tops cells up.
why: Kills destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): per-useful-bit read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.1-0.3 pJ; also removes row-activation hammer stress.
note: Subthreshold partial read gives non-destructive 64B access; needs ~0.2 fF local sense nodes and precise sip control across Vt spread.

title: Vertical charge-coupled columns store packets without access transistors
idea: Deposit a 3D-NAND-like gate stack around a single-crystal or recrystallized channel and clock the gate tiers in three phases to shift charge packets up the column to one sense node at the top, so 128 bits share one transistor and no capacitor.
why: Leakage physics: a buried potential well loses charge only by thermal generation, far below a transistor off-state tail (fact 3), and removing the per-cell capacitor sidesteps the charge wall (fact 1); a 128-deep shift at ~1 ns per step keeps access near DRAM class while density follows tier count.
note: 128 bits per sense node with no capacitor; doubts: transfer inefficiency in poly channels, shift energy and serial latency.

title: Vertical charge-coupled strings store 64 bits per pillar without capacitors
idea: A bit is just a charge packet and needs only a potential well, not a capacitor plus transistor. Use NAND-like vertical pillars whose tiered gates clock 3-phase wells that shift packets to one sense amplifier at the pillar top: 192 tiers give 64 bits per pillar at 60 nm pitch.
why: ~56 nm2/bit (~15x today) with one contact per 64 bits; deletes per-cell capacitor dielectric (Zr/Hf), tungsten contacts and EUV. Transfer inefficiency and serial latency are the risks.
note: Capacitorless vertical CCD shift strings give ~15x density; poly-channel leakage, transfer loss over 64 shifts and serial latency are doubts.

title: Compressed-sensing readout makes selector-less crossbars usable
idea: The cheapest possible cell is a two-terminal resistor at a wire crossing with no transistor or selector, but sneak paths forbid single-cell reads. Read a whole 1k x 1k tile with pseudo-random row voltage patterns, measure column currents, and let a decoder in the interface chiplet solve the linear system (with sparse coding and block parity) to recover every bit.
why: 8-16 stacked BEOL crossbar layers at 4F^2 with 2-3 masks each could approach ~100x cheaper per GB; trades latency (us tile decode), energy and endurance.
note: Decoding summed currents needs high ADC precision against IR drop; resistive endurance not DRAM-class.

title: Vertical 3D charge-coupled shift-register memory with one regenerator per string
idea: Po: the bit is a rumor passed down a line. Store charge packets in potential wells along a tall vertical channel with dozens of stacked gate layers (3D NAND-like tiers clocked as a CCD); packets shift up and down and only the end-of-string regenerating sense amp restores them, so refresh is the shifting itself, with no per-bit capacitor or access transistor.
why: Facts 2, 4 and 7: reuses 3D NAND tier deposition (no EUV per tier, density scales with tier count); access becomes 100 ns-1 us block access, suited to tensor streams.
note: 3D NAND tiers clocked as a CCD avoid per-bit transistors; poly-Si transfer efficiency, dark current and serial access are doubts.

title: Origami artist: roll one flat DRAM membrane into twenty tiers
idea: An origami artist turns a flat sheet into volume. Pattern one 2D cell array on a strained bilayer nanomembrane (e.g., SiN/SiGe) over a sacrificial layer; on release, built-in strain rolls it into a tight Swiss roll of ~20 turns, so one 2D lithography pass yields 20 tiers, with wordlines running along the roll and contacted at its edge.
why: Gets 3D density (fact 2) from 2D lithography, avoiding 26-tier stack deposition and deep etch; litho cost per bit falls ~1/N with N turns. Speculative: turn-to-turn registration, heat removal, edge contacts.
note: 20 tiers from one 2D pass; turn registration, edge contacts and heat removal are unsolved.

title: Optane's crosspoint kept, PCM swapped for selector-gated capacitor
idea: Optane died largely on cost and PCM endurance, but its stacked crosspoint and OTS selector worked. Place a tiny MIM capacitor in series with the OTS at each crosspoint: the selector's threshold snap acts as a transistor-free access device, turning the array into a refreshed 4F2 multi-deck DRAM.
why: 4F2 per deck with stackable decks and no lateral transistor (Fact 2); reuses idle chalcogenide PVD tooling. Risk: OTS sub-threshold leakage must reach ~fA.
note: Transistor-free multi-deck DRAM; OTS off-leakage needs fA-level, orders below demonstrated, and holding-current behavior complicates writes.

title: Fairchild CCD memory reborn as vertical IGZO buried-channel CCD
idea: 1970s CCD memories died from serial access and silicon dark current that filled potential wells within ms when hot. Stack 64-128 gate tiers 3D-NAND-style around a vertical IGZO channel, store electron packets under alternate gates and shift a few stages to a top sense node. IGZO has no holes to invert the channel and a ~3.1 eV gap, so thermal generation stays negligible at 125 C and packets last seconds or more.
why: 3D DRAM with no capacitor and no per-tier transistor (Fact 2), ~10x bits per litho layer; retention far beyond 64 ms even at 125 C.
note: Capacitorless 3D DRAM: packets shift along tiers; doubt is IGZO charge-transfer efficiency with traps and serial latency.

title: Optane's selector drift turned into DRAM retention
idea: In 3D XPoint, the ovonic threshold switch's threshold voltage drifted upward with log-time after each firing, which eroded read margins. Use two back-to-back OTS films as the access device of a crosspoint 1S1C capacitor cell. After each access the threshold drifts up, so the selector's off-state leakage falls as the stored bit ages. Each access or refresh re-fires the selector, which resets its state.
why: Transistor-free, stackable 4F2 crosspoint DRAM (attacks the 3D DRAM blocker and litho cost). Because drift makes leakage fall over time instead of sitting at a fixed tail, refresh is claimed to be ~10x longer than in half-select-limited crosspoint designs.
note: Drift-as-feature is clever, but OTS off-leakage sits ~1e6x above fA retention needs; stackable transistorless DRAM if solved.

title: Snapback counting reads N stacked threshold cells per crosspoint
idea: Failure mined: Optane died partly because each extra deck needed its own lithography and decoders, so cost never scaled past two decks. Fix: deposit 8 chalcogenide threshold-switching memory layers in series at every crosspoint, pattern them with one etch, and engineer a different threshold window for each layer. One voltage ramp per pillar is read by counting and timing the snapback current spikes, whose pattern encodes all 8 states.
why: 10x at the same cost: 8 bits per 4F^2 crosspoint vs 1 bit per 6F^2 is ~12x density, with one patterning step and one decoder set shared by all 8 layers, so decks no longer multiply masks.
note: 8 OTS layers per crosspoint with one etch could give ~12x density; doubt: Vth variability across 8 windows, read disturb, endurance.

title: Zettacore redox molecules: eight built-in reference levels per cell
idea: Failure mined: Zettacore's porphyrin molecular memory stored charge in discrete oxidation states but died on CMOS process heat and slow voltammetric reads. Fix: after the 400 C steps, graft thermally robust ferrocene/porphyrin mixtures with 7 redox couples onto a nanoporous TiN electrode. The sense amp's reference ladder is a reference electrode coated with the same molecules, so the potential plateaus self-calibrate and each cell stores 3 bits.
why: 10x at the same cost: 3 bits per cell x a crosspoint-compatible 4F^2 footprint (the porous electrode supplies ~50 fF-equivalent charge) x fewer reference generators = ~9-12x vs 1 bit per 6F^2. The molecules cost pennies per wafer.
note: Multi-redox molecules self-calibrate 3-bit levels; thermal budget, kinetics and endurance are major doubts.

title: Plasma-display memory effect: global sustain waveform replaces refresh and transistors
idea: Failure mined: plasma displays held each pixel's state as wall charge under a global AC sustain waveform, with only row and column drivers and no per-pixel transistor, and lost to LCD and OLED on power. Fix: each crosspoint cell pairs a thin threshold switch with a small capacitor in a hysteresis loop. A global sustain clock re-pumps every 1 cell while 0 cells never fire, and coincident row/column pulses set or clear individual cells.
why: 10x at the same cost: no access transistor, refresh controller or refresh bandwidth. 4F^2 cells in 4 self-aligned decks sharing lines (~6x) x periphery shrinking to ~20% (~1.6x) = ~10x.
note: Plasma-style global sustain removes access transistor and refresh; selector endurance under constant sustain firing and read path are the doubts.

title: Charge-injection-device cells: two-gate X-Y charge storage with non-destructive reads
idea: Failure mined: GE's charge-injection device (CID) imager lost to CCDs, yet it had an X-Y addressed, transistor-free pixel of two coupled MOS gates, read non-destructively by moving charge between the gates and sensing the column. Fix: use CID pairs as memory cells, with the row gate and column gate overlapping one storage well. A write injects charge; a read shifts it under the column gate and back, so the charge never leaves the well and can be re-read for multi-level sensing.
why: 10x at the same cost: a transistor-free ~4F^2 cell (1.5x) x 3 bits per well from averaged non-destructive re-reads (3x) x no restore and much less periphery (~2x) = ~9-10x, using planar CMOS-image-sensor processing.
note: Transistor-free X-Y well with nondestructive re-reads; doubt: thermal generation fills wells fast and column signal is tiny.

title: ZettaCore's molecular redox storage repurposed as a charge-multiplying capacitor coating
idea: ZettaCore stored charge in porphyrin redox molecules on silicon but died on the 400C BEOL thermal budget. Graft thermally stable inorganic redox clusters (polyoxometalates) inside each 3D DRAM capacitor. Each cluster stores several electrons at a fixed potential, adding pseudocapacitance on top of the dielectric's.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 5-10x charge per um2 lets 3D tiers use short, low-AR capacitors (fact 2).
note: Redox clusters multiply charge per area; doubt: ns-scale Faradaic kinetics, retention, and endurance.

title: Josephson-era missing memory: 77 K thin-oxide 3D NAND as DRAM
idea: IBM's Josephson program (cancelled 1983) and later cryogenic computing stalled for lack of dense, cheap cold memory. At 77 K leakage collapses, so a 3D NAND-style vertical string with a 1.5-2 nm direct-tunneling oxide instead of ~7 nm Fowler-Nordheim oxide programs at ~3-5 V in tens of ns, suffers little hot-carrier wear and holds charge for hours.
why: Meets 100x: NAND cost structure (~$0.03-0.08/GB) with near-DRAM write speed, refresh-free hours retention and ~1e12-class endurance. Trade: liquid-nitrogen cooling (~10-15% facility overhead).
note: NAND cost with near-DRAM writes; doubt: direct tunneling through 2 nm oxide is temperature-insensitive, so hours retention is unlikely.

title: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D antifuse stack made rewritable with selector-charged capacitors
idea: Matrix Semiconductor's 3D poly-diode antifuse memory (bought by SanDisk in 2005) stacked cheaply at ~4 masks per layer but died for being write-once. Keep the stacked poly pillar process and swap the antifuse for a small planar MIM capacitor charged through a bidirectional punch-through n-p-n selector, giving 1S1C dynamic cells with unlimited endurance, refreshed like DRAM.
why: Meets 100x: no access transistor, no high-AR capacitor, 8-16 DUV decks; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: selector leakage forces ms-scale refresh, higher refresh power, thin sense margin.
note: No transistor per bit, ~$0.1/GB; poly punch-through selector leakage and half-select disturb likely kill retention.

title: Kovio's liquid-silicon ink printed into 32 cheap gain-cell tiers
idea: Kovio printed silicon RFID from liquid cyclopentasilane and folded in 2014 on a tiny market and hard-to-handle pyrophoric ink. Inside a sealed inert coater module, spin 20 nm silicon films from ink, crystallize only the top film with a nanosecond laser, and stack 32 tiers of poly-Si 2T gain cells, each tier patterned by one imprint.
why: Meets 100x: each tier costs a spin, a laser scan and one imprint (~$5-10/wafer) instead of epitaxy or transfer; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: grain-boundary leakage forces ms refresh and defect mapping.
note: Spin-on Si tiers at ~$5-10/wafer each; grain-boundary leakage and ms refresh likely erode DRAM-class value.

title: Hitachi's single-electron grain memory stacked in 64 cheap tiers
idea: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano, 1990s) stored a few electrons in grains of 3-4 nm polysilicon and died because random grains caused wild threshold scatter. Tame the scatter with per-cell write-verify calibration and a 3-cell majority code, and exploit its simplicity of thin films with no capacitor or deep etch by depositing 64 tiers gated by one shared vertical-gate hole pattern.
why: Meets 100x: tiers are just thin depositions, writes are fast direct tunneling (~10s of ns), retention minutes to hours; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: 3x cell redundancy, calibration time, variability.
note: Thin-film tiers with no capacitor could hit ~$0.1/GB; doubt: grain threshold scatter despite write-verify and 3x redundancy.

title: Redox pseudocapacitor nanocell replaces 70:1 pillar with planar charge sponge
idea: Effect walk: Faradaic surface redox (pseudocapacitance). Replace the dielectric capacitor with a 5-nm hydrous RuO2 or Ti3C2 MXene film against a nanometre solid proton conductor; fast surface redox stores ~100-1000 uF/cm2 versus ~7 uF/cm2 for ZrO2, so a flat 30x30 nm pad holds ~4-5 fF at 0.5 V.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) with no AR 60-75 etch, removing the deep-etch/deposition module (~30-50% of capacitor cost); risks are self-discharge and whether surface redox keeps up at ns timescales.
note: Planar 4-5 fF pad removes the pillar; pseudocap kinetics are ms-scale and self-discharge is high.

title: Room-temperature single-electron electrometer at every vertical bitline foot
idea: Coulomb blockade: a sub-3 nm silicon island single-electron transistor, formed by self-limiting fin oxidation, sits at the base of each vertical bitline as a charge electrometer that can resolve ~10 electrons. Lateral 3D tier capacitors can then hold 0.2 fF instead of 5 fF, because the read no longer depends on charge-sharing against a large bitline capacitance.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) that blocks thin 3D tiers (fact 2); claim 20x smaller Cs, so planar tier capacitors become viable.
note: RT Coulomb-blockade readout could cut Cs 20x; doubt: sub-3 nm island variability and offset charge across billions of bitlines.

title: Accordion-folded single membrane becomes 26 tiers of crystalline cells
idea: Process one planar single-crystal membrane (SOI device layer) with lateral access transistors in a strip pattern, release it, then fold it accordion-style like a road map using prestressed hinge lines. N folds yield N tiers that all came from one high-quality planar process.
why: Fact 2: gives 3D DRAM single-crystal lateral transistors for every tier while using only planar processing once. Folding replaces 26x deposition/etch loops.
note: Folding gives tiers but no dense inter-tier contacts or nm alignment; micron tier pitch caps density.

title: Gen-10.5 display-glass panels stacked with twenty tiers of oxide-TFT DRAM
idea: Ideal: memory sold like window glass. Closest: use Gen-10.5 display lines (~9.9 m2 panels) to build 2T0C/1T1C tiers from In-free ZnSnO TFTs, Mo/Al lines and planar Al2O3/TiO2 caps (TFT off-current ~1e-21 A/um makes small caps adequate), 4-5 masks per tier with panel nanoimprint at F~0.25 um, 20 tiers stacked at <=350 C.
why: 100x: panel processing ~$25/m2 per tier vs ~$150k/m2 for leading DRAM wafers; at ~0.5 um2/bit (~250 GB/m2/tier) x 20 tiers = 5 TB/m2 for ~$500 -> ~$0.1/GB vs ~$10/GB today. Trades latency (100-300 ns), volume and power; zero EUV, W, Hf, He.
note: Display-line tiers could cut slow-tier $/GB ~10x; doubts: 20-tier yield, panel nanoimprint overlay, 100-300 ns latency.

title: Vertical charge-coupled shift strings: memory without per-bit transistors
idea: Ideal: memory with no transistor, capacitor or contact per bit. Closest: in a 3D-NAND-like stack, clock tier wordlines three-phase so charge packets move along a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel like a CCD; each string is a shift register read by one sense amp at its foot, with a regeneration stage every ~32 tiers to cancel transfer loss.
why: 100x: deletes the cell capacitor, contacts and leakage tail (Facts 1-3), uses only Si/O/N/Mo, and scales density with tier count at ~3D-NAND cost (~$0.05/GB). Trades serial access (~100-300 ns per 64-stage shift, hidden by bank interleaving) and charge-transfer efficiency.
note: Charge-transfer efficiency in trap-rich amorphous oxide channels is the killer doubt.

title: Ion-beam ripple self-patterning writes wafer-wide nanoline arrays without masks
idea: Ideal: line arrays that appear by themselves under a flood beam. Closest: off-normal low-energy Ar+ sputtering of an a-Si or metal hard-mask film spontaneously forms Bradley-Harper ripples at 20-40 nm wavelength, phase-locked by a coarse pre-pattern; transfer them as wordline/bitline gratings and repeat rotated 90 degrees for the crossing grid.
why: 100x: pattern formation costs one broad-beam ion-source step (tens of $k tooling) instead of SAQP/EUV, cutting array patterning per layer >50x and enabling ~$0.1/GB in multi-tier stacks; trades long-range order and line-edge roughness.
note: Maskless self-organized gratings could slash patterning cost; long-range order and LER are far from DRAM specs.

title: Vertical oxide CCD string: transistor-less 3D charge-shift memory
idea: Etch one high-aspect-ratio hole through 128-256 alternating W/Mo and SiO2 word planes (the same module as 3D NAND), and line it with a thin gate oxide and an ALD IGZO/IGO channel. Clock planes in 4 phases (2 gates per bit): each bit is a packet of ~1,000-5,000 electrons in an accumulation well. Si CCDs lose stored charge to thermal generation (dark current); wide-gap IGZO generates essentially no carriers, so packets hold, limited only by inter-well barriers and gate leakage. Reading shifts packets out of the top of the string into a charge-transfer sense amp (B1-04) on bonded periphery, and data recirculates to the bottom: a delay-line memory with 32-64-bit strings and thousands of parallel holes per line access. Planes are segmented into small blocks to keep plane RC at ~1 ns per phase.
why: 4.2-8.3x 1b density (1.85-3.7 Gb/mm2 at 128-256 planes) with zero per-bit devices; streaming read energy 17-67 fJ/bit; but access is serial (32-128 ns worst-case to a given bit).
note: Transistor-less charge-shift strings on NAND tooling; doubts: IGZO trap states hurting transfer efficiency, and serial access latency.

title: Nanogap (vacuum/air) tunnel-barrier floating node: flash-like retention without oxide wear
idea: The floating metal node (TiN or W, anchored on dielectric on one side) faces a write electrode across a 2.5-4 nm gap. The gap is made by removing an ALD sacrificial layer (carbon or Al2O3) and then sealed, like BEOL air-gaps or NASA's nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors, which work in air because the gap is far below the ~70 nm mean free path. The node is the gate of an IGZO or Si read transistor (2T-like gain cell), so the read is non-destructive. Writing uses field emission at a few V/nm (field enhancement 2-3 at edges); holding relies on the exponential non-linearity of tunnelling. Charge never passes through a solid dielectric, so there are no trap generation, SILC or charge-to-breakdown limits, the mechanisms that cap flash endurance at ~1e5. Low-work-function coatings (LaB6-class, 2.7 eV) cut write voltage, but even plain TiN (4.5 eV) works at 8 V.
why: [SPECULATIVE] A non-volatile, refresh-free DRAM-class gain cell: retention 3.7e4 s (2.5 nm gap, 2.7 eV) to >1e8 s (3 nm), writes in 0.4-40 ns. Endurance is not set by oxide damage, with a target of >=1e12.
note: Charge never crosses a solid dielectric, removing oxide-wear endurance limits; doubt: sealing reproducible 2.5-4 nm gaps given exponential gap sensitivity.

title: Magnify tiers 300x: convert idle 3D NAND fabs to gain-cell lines
idea: Reuse 3D NAND tool sets (alternating film stacks, one deep channel-hole etch, staircase contacts) to build 300-500 tier vertical-channel IGZO 2T0C gain cells, with a string-select scheme giving random access per tier and aggressive refresh.
why: NAND reached ~$0.05/GB through deposition-defined stacking instead of lithography; borrowing its fab economics targets ~$0.1/GB DRAM-class memory (~100x), trading latency (~100 ns+) and refresh energy, while monetizing underused NAND capacity.
note: NAND-style deposition stacking could give >10x cost/bit; random access per tier and IGZO vertical-channel uniformity at 300+ tiers are big doubts.

title: Crested-barrier capacitor: the capacitor is its own access switch
idea: Inverts 'storage and switch are separate devices': each crossbar node is a floating metal nanolayer between two crested tunnel barriers (e.g., nitride/AlN/nitride trilayers) whose peak collapses at high field, giving ~10^12 current change between the ~3 V write and ~1 V hold; charge on the floating layer is the bit, written in ns by tunneling and read capacitively, from one blanket deposition per deck.
why: No transistor, no capacitor tower, one deposition per deck in 4F2 crossbar stacks, ~100x cheaper per GB; crested barriers reduce oxide stress, aiming at 10^12+ endurance; trade-off: write energy and unproven endurance.
note: Transistor-free, capacitor-tower-free 4F2 decks from blanket depositions would cut cost/bit >10x; doubt: capacitive crossbar readout and 1e12 write/hold contrast.

title: Biologist's self-assembly: block copolymers draw 5 nm cells
idea: Cells build structures by self-assembly. High-chi silicon-containing block copolymers on sparse ArF guide patterns define a 10 nm-pitch hexagonal array of vertical nanowire access transistors, each with an oxide-semiconductor storage node instead of a capacitor. Spin-coat and anneal from U.S. chemical suppliers replace 5-7 EUV layers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 at F=5 nm vs 6F^2 at 12 nm is ~8.6x; with periphery under the array, ~10x/mm^2. Spin-and-bake costs far less than EUV, so wafer cost stays flat; DSA defectivity is the big risk.
note: 10 nm-pitch DSA vertical access plus storage node would be ~10x density; defectivity and contacting at 5 nm are huge doubts.

title: Rail yard master: racetrack memory built in U.S. hard-disk head fabs
idea: A rail yard master moves cars along sidings instead of building a track for each car. Magnetic domain-wall racetrack memory uses vertical U-shaped nanowires, each holding ~64 domains shifted by current past one read/write head. It is built in U.S. hard-disk read-head fabs, which already pattern 20 nm magnetic multilayers in volume and are losing HDD demand.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 bits per ~4F^2 track footprint is ~10-20x DRAM areal density. The head fabs are depreciated, domain-wall motion does not wear out, and shift latency is tens of ns; pinning and shift errors are the risks.
note: Head-fab reuse is clever, but vertical racetrack has stalled for 15+ years on pinning and shift errors.

title: All-IGZO monolithic memory: n-only periphery in the same tiers
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: build sense amps, decoders and drivers from the same IGZO transistors as the 2T0C array, using bootstrapped n-only (pseudo-CMOS) circuits, so each BEOL tier is a complete memory with no CMOS underneath. The whole stack can sit on any logic die's metal stack.
why: Fact 5 and 7: memory micrometres above compute (~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM) and periphery needs no separate FEOL; any logic fab's BEOL becomes DRAM capacity.
note: Any logic BEOL becomes DRAM capacity; doubt: n-only IGZO sense amps are slow, variable and low-density.

title: One latent per token regenerates every layer's K/V on demand
idea: Inverts 'each layer stores its own KV cache': DRAM holds a single low-rank latent per token (e.g., 256 dims), and each layer's tensor cores up-project it to K and V just in time inside the attention kernel, spending cheap FLOPs to save scarce bytes. A short distillation pass retrofits existing models so the shared cross-layer latent is trained jointly.
why: KV-cache bytes drop 10-40x vs per-layer FP16 KV, beyond per-layer latent attention, so long-context serving fits in a fraction of the HBM/DRAM.
note: 10-40x KV cut if one latent serves all layers; doubt: retrofit by short distillation; MLA/CLA partly there.

title: Ultra-wide-gap amorphous Ga2O3 storage node holding 0.1 fF for hours
idea: Generation leakage scales as ni ~ exp(-Eg/2kT), so moving from IGZO (3.2 eV) to RT-sputtered a-Ga2O3 (4.8 eV) cuts intrinsic generation by ~1e13. A 0.1 fF planar MIM node behind an a-Ga2O3 access device then holds a 0.3 V signal for >1e4 s, read by a local gain transistor.
why: Shrinks the capacitor ~50x (fact 1) and removes refresh (fact 3) in a planar BEOL-stackable cell, going beyond the IGZO prior work. The risk is defect-limited (not intrinsic) leakage in amorphous films.
note: Ga2O3 beyond IGZO for refresh-free BEOL gain cell; defect-state leakage and very low a-Ga2O3 mobility are the doubts.

title: Correlated double sampling sense amps read 0.2 fF cells
idea: Sample the bitline before and after charge sharing onto two capacitors in a logic-process sense amp and amplify the difference, cancelling offset and 1/f noise so the required signal approaches the sqrt(kT/C) floor instead of a 6-sigma mismatch margin.
why: First principles: sqrt(kT/C) for a 30 fF bitline is ~0.37 mV, so ~3 mV suffices versus ~80-100 mV today; Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~0.2-0.5 fF, dissolving the charge wall (fact 1) and enabling lateral capacitors in 3D (fact 2).
note: CDS sense amp targets kT/C floor so Cs drops ~10x; doubt: WL/BL coupling and charge injection, not thermal noise, set the floor.

title: All-oxide CMOS periphery lets memory panels need no silicon chips
idea: Ideal: periphery made from the same cheap film as the cells. Closest: build sense amps, decoders and refresh logic from complementary oxide TFTs (n-ZnSnO with p-SnO or p-Cu2O, all abundant, <=300 C) using bootstrapped dynamic logic to compensate the weak p-FET, so panel memory needs no bonded silicon driver ICs.
why: 100x enabler: periphery is ~49% of DRAM die (Fact 7); moving it onto ~$30/m2 panel layers is required to reach ~$0.1/GB. Trades sensing speed (50-200 ns) and power.
note: Required enabler for panel memory; weak p-type oxide TFTs limit sense speed, margin and power.

title: Poor man's HBM on commercial HDI substrates
idea: Substitute the silicon interposer with a commercial mSAP HDI board (15 um lines) carrying bare LPDDR5X dies flip-chipped within 3 mm of an FPGA/ASIC, running a 1024-bit bus at a modest 2-3 Gb/s per pin.
why: Cost per bit and capital: roughly HBM2-class bandwidth at LPDDR cost without TSVs or scarce CoWoS capacity.

title: Second-life DRAM: retired server DIMMs reborn as CXL pools
idea: Eliminate new wafers for the capacity tier: strip DDR4/DDR5 chips from decommissioned servers, screen with burn-in and row-hammer tests, and mount them behind CXL Type-3 controllers that translate protocol and map out weak rows.
why: Huge volumes of DRAM are retired yearly; reusing it as a slower tier raises usable supply with zero fab capex and spares new DDR5/HBM for hot data, at ~5-10x lower cost/bit than today's 4x contract price.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL; chip-level harvesting adds screening cost.

title: Prior action: base-die gather engine packs sparse reads before PHY
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: the HBM base die runs a scatter-gather and transpose engine. The GPU sends index lists (KV-cache page tables, embedding IDs, MoE token routes), and the base die collects 32 B sectors across banks and packs them into dense full-width bursts before they cross the PHY.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): 2-8x fewer wasted bits cross the interface on sparse access, and effective bandwidth rises by the same factor.

title: Discarding and recovering: partial-good HBM stacks sold as lower tiers
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: instead of scrapping stacks with one bad tier or weak TSV lanes, fuse out the bad tier or half the lanes in the base die and re-bin the stacks as 8-high or half-width parts for inference cards and edge devices. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: HBM yield (fact 6): turns the 20-30% yield loss into a sellable lower tier, effectively +10-20% usable HBM supply from the same wafers.

title: Secondary-market DDR4 reborn in CXL memory expansion boxes
idea: Box: reclaimed DDR4 DIMMs x standard x standard x CXL controller with per-rank ECC remap and aging-aware refresh x refurbished chassis x refurbishment line. DDR4 from decommissioned servers is tested, graded and re-hosted behind CXL controllers that hide its latency for tier-2 data.
why: Supply: capacity with zero new wafers; tens of PB of DDR4 retire each year; cost per GB ~20-30% of new DDR5.
note: Retired DDR4 behind CXL already piloted by hyperscalers; solid but known.

title: Hash-deduplicating base die stores shared KV prefixes once
idea: Worsen: store the same system-prompt KV cache separately for every user. Flip: the memory base die hashes each 4 KB block on write and keeps a content-addressed table, so identical prefix blocks across users map to one physical copy with copy-on-write, transparent to the host.
why: Usable capacity: 2-5x more effective KV capacity per GB for chat inference with shared prompts and agents.
note: Prefix sharing already done in host software (vLLM); hardware dedup adds modest novelty.

title: IBM MXT fixed: compression lives in the CXL link, not the core
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled effective capacity with hardware compression but died from decompression latency on the CPU critical path, a large L3 requirement and OS changes. Put a 2-4 ns base-delta/zero-run compressor with a metadata cache inside the CXL memory controller, present the OS a fixed larger capacity, and compress only far-tier lines so hot data never pays the latency.
why: Do DRAM's job with less, and link energy: server data typically compresses 1.5-2.5x, so 33-60% fewer DRAM bits for the same capacity and fewer bits crossing the link.
note: CXL-controller compression already commercialized/proposed (e.g., ZeroPoint).

title: Index-list gather engine returns only packed useful words
idea: Ideal: the memory already knows which words you need. Closest achievable: the host sends a list of 4-8 byte indices (embedding rows, sparse nonzeros, KV pages) over the command path, and the base die does bank-parallel fetches and returns densely packed 64 B lines holding only the requested words.
why: Fact 8 and fact 5: sparse and embedding workloads waste 80-95% of transferred bytes; packing cuts interface traffic 5-10x for those patterns.

title: Second-life DRAM: re-certify decommissioned server dies under strong ECC
idea: Worse: shred millions of 3-5 year old DIMMs while new bits cost 4x more. Flip: industrial lines recover modules from retired servers, run deep retention and hammer profiling, and resell them graded into tiers behind controllers with chipkill plus elastic refresh for cold or secondary memory pools.
why: Supply and scarce resources: part of the installed base (tens of exabytes) could return as CXL capacity tiers using zero new wafers.

title: Defect-budget co-design: 100x pattern-defect tolerance to unlock cheap patterning
idea: Every 128-bit word carries 16 BCH (t=2) check bits instead of 8 SECDED bits, decoded in fast logic-process periphery (bonded or under-array). A small CAM remaps the few residual failing words found at test; mat-level sparing (NAND bad-block style) handles clustered pattern defects (line opens, shorts). Retention-weak cells are remapped too. This turns patterning defectivity from a yield killer into a few percent of area overhead.
why: Random-defect tolerance x100 (p 1e-6 -> 1e-4) for +6.25% extra check bits and ~65 remap words per 16 Gb die.

title: Lifetime-leased refresh: streamed and dead data are never refreshed
idea: A lease table in the memory controller (or HBM base die) puts each 2 MB region in one of three classes. (i) 'Dead': freed pages, retired KV. (ii) 'Streamed with period <= P': weights and live KV in LLM decode, read every token. (iii) 'Normal'. Class (ii) rows are restored as a side effect of every full activation. A per-region activation timestamp certifies that each row was opened within tREF, and the controller issues a targeted refresh only for rows that miss the deadline. Class (i) rows get no refresh at all. For most of an inference HBM, the all-bank REF command and its tRFC blackout disappear. A further step is an HBM bin specified for 'access-guaranteed' use, with a relaxed retention screen. Dies that fail today's 32 ms retention test become usable for weights.
why: Refresh energy -> ~0 for streamed and dead regions, and 5-15% more usable HBM bandwidth in bandwidth-bound decode (x1.05-1.18 tokens/s), with no cell change. General servers with 30-50% dead memory get refresh energy x0.5-0.7.

title: HBF weight tier with read-disturb-aware 'weight mode'
idea: HBF stacks NAND dies on TSVs behind an HBM-like interface (OCP spec August 2026: 256 GB/die, 512 GB per 16-high stack, ~1.6 TB/s read). Weights are written once per deployment, while KV and activations stay in DRAM. Each decode step reads every weight page, so a page sees 1e5-3e6 reads per day. Read disturb (pass-voltage stress on the unselected wordlines of a block) then forces periodic reclaim, that is, a rewrite. The 'weight mode' has four parts: program weights in pSLC, or TLC with relaxed retention; interleave each tensor across many blocks so read counts stay even; track per-block read counters and relocate before the disturb limit; and keep a second replica on another die to alternate reads when the disturb budget is tight.
why: HBF claims 8-16x HBM capacity at similar cost. In endurance-safe pSLC weight mode it still gives ~3-5x HBM capacity per $, against HBM's ~3x DDR5 wafer cost per bit.

title: Compact-then-sleep: compress, pack, partial-array self-refresh
idea: The memory controller (phone SoC or server CXL controller) carries a hardware compaction engine. When it detects idle, it walks live pages, LZ4-compresses them (2-3x is typical for Marvell-class engines), packs them into the lowest segments and updates a remap table. It then issues partial-array self-refresh (PASR) masks that leave the vacated segments unrefreshed. Combined with B4-02's ECC-stretched self-refresh interval (1 s at 85 C, longer when cool). On wake, pages decompress on first touch (us-scale, like a minor fault) or eagerly in the background.
why: Idle refresh power /2-3 from compaction alone, and /32-48 with ECC-stretched self-refresh: a 64 GB RDIMM drops from 0.49 W to 10-15 mW.

title: Magnify DIMM lifespan 3x via a reclamation exchange
idea: Hyperscalers retire servers every 4-6 years with healthy DIMMs; robotic test-and-rebin centers grade them (retention, row-hammer threshold, speed) and repackage them into CXL Type-3 memory-expander sleds resold as a capacity tier with a 3-year warranty.
why: Supply without a fab: ~10-15% of annual server DRAM demand could be served by reused modules at ~20-30% of new price.

title: Page-age compression ladder across ns-to-hour timescales
idea: Time-scale tiering: hardware in the CXL expander compresses pages by idle age. Pages idle for 1 s get LZ4, 1 min gets zstd with dictionary, and 1 h gets deduplicated, compressed and parked in flash, while hot pages stay raw.
why: Most of a fleet's DRAM holds data idle for seconds or more. The ladder lifts effective capacity 1.6-2.5x, a supply gain that is purely logic.

title: OMI done right: generation-agnostic CXL buffer reuses retired DDR4
idea: IBM's OpenCAPI Memory Interface (and FB-DIMM before it) died tied to one CPU vendor and one buffer supplier. Fix: an open CXL Type-3 card whose buffer drives DDR3, DDR4 or DDR5 on its back side, so DIMMs pulled from retired servers go back into new servers behind CXL, with the buffer adding ECC and patrol scrub to manage aged parts.
why: Reuse: hyperscalers retire very large volumes of working DDR4 each year; a second 4-5-year life could add ~20-30% to usable supply at ~10-20% of the cost of new bits.

title: Memory refinery ASIC: one uniform pool from mixed-vintage used DIMMs
idea: Ideal: all old memory looks like new memory. Closest achievable at trailing nodes: a 28 nm CXL controller with DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 PHYs, chipkill ECC across heterogeneous ranks, per-device health telemetry and hot-page migration to the fastest devices turns decommissioned DIMMs into a qualified capacity tier.
why: Reuse: EBs of DDR4 retire in server refreshes; recovered at ~30% of the cost per GB of new.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL; FPGA-provable.

title: Cuban mechanic's almendron: keep old DDR4 alive behind CXL
idea: Havana mechanics keep 1950s cars running with improvised parts. In the same spirit, low-cost CXL Type-3 bridge cards each host 8-16 retired DDR4 RDIMMs and give new DDR5 servers a second-life capacity tier. The controller adds chipkill-class ECC and runs the DDR4 at reduced speed so it lasts longer.
why: Reuse supply: hyperscalers retire tens of millions of DDR4 DIMMs a year; reusing them could displace 10-20% of new DDR5 purchases for capacity-bound workloads, at ~150 ns extra latency.
note: Already deployed by hyperscalers (e.g., Azure CXL DDR4 reuse).

title: Cross-generation CXL reuse of retired DDR4 as tier-2 memory
idea: Time shift of DIMM life: a CXL controller with a DDR4 back end and strong symbol ECC lets hyperscalers move DDR4 pulled from retired servers into CXL boxes attached to new DDR5-only CPUs.
why: Delays e-waste of DIMMs with plenty of life left by 4-6 years. Covers 20-30% of new-server capacity needs without new bits.
note: Already deployed by hyperscalers (DDR4 behind CXL).

title: Substitute harvested second-life DRAM for newly fabricated bits
idea: Industrialize take-back of retired server DIMMs: robotic desoldering, at-speed retest with per-row retention profiling, and re-binning into CXL memory-expander cards for tier-2 memory, with controller ECC and adaptive refresh hiding weak cells.
why: A reused bit needs essentially zero fab water versus ~0.3-1 L per new Gb, a >100x cut per delivered bit, and it adds usable supply immediately during the shortage.
note: Hyperscalers already pool reused DDR4 behind CXL; scaling reverse logistics is the play.

title: Stranded-memory exchange: CXL fabric rents idle DRAM across racks
idea: Inverts 'memory belongs to one server': a row-scale CXL 3 memory fabric plus a spot-market scheduler leases the ~25-35% of installed DRAM that sits stranded to other servers by the minute, with prices that steer tenants.
why: Raises usable supply ~20-30% with no new wafers, offsetting the 4x price spike; materials per useful bit fall by the same factor.

title: Hollow-fiber sieving plus pressure swing recaptures fab helium as service
idea: Effect: helium's 2.6 angstrom kinetic diameter lets it permeate polyimide hollow fibers ~100x faster than N2 or Ar. Capture exhaust at chucks, load locks and leak stations, enrich it to 90% through membranes, finish it to 5N by pressure-swing adsorption and refill on site, all sold as helium-as-a-service.
why: Helium chokepoint: 70-90% recovery cuts virgin helium purchases ~5-10x and protects fabs from Qatar-type outages.
note: Membrane+PSA recovery is commercial; service model twist.

title: CXL bridges give retired DDR4 modules a second decade
idea: Scale shift from server to rack: when servers retire after 4-5 years, keep their DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs and seat them in CXL memory-expander cards. The cards use controllers built on existing 28 nm logic lines and serve a far-memory tier at ~150-250 ns.
why: Turns hyperscaler retirements (exabytes per year) into supply with zero new wafers. Every reused bit avoids all of its fab helium, tungsten and water.
note: Already deployed by hyperscalers (DDR4 behind CXL).

title: Via-programmed ROM for frozen model weights frees DRAM
idea: Combine mask-ROM economics with AI inference: weights frozen for a product's life are encoded in one via layer (1-2F2 per bit, multi-level via resistance for 2 bits) on a die whose other masks are shared, so only the via mask changes per model, written by e-beam or DUV. The weights never need refresh, never wear out, and stop occupying HBM.
why: Weights are a large share of inference memory; moving them to refresh-free ROM at ~1/5 the cost per bit releases that DRAM supply.
note: Hardwired-model silicon already pursued (e.g., Taalas); model churn limits benefit.

title: Apollo core-rope ROM reborn as via-coupled multi-layer weight store
idea: Apollo's rope memory encoded bits as whether a sense wire threaded a core. Encode frozen AI weights as presence or absence of via stubs coupling word lines to sense lines across 8 metal-layer pairs of an existing 40-nm logic process (one custom via mask per layer); pulsing a word line induces charge only on sense lines with a stub, so there is no DC sneak path.
why: Frees DRAM/HBM now spent on immutable weights; no refresh, no capacitor; 8 planes x 4F2 at 40 nm is ~800 nm2 per bit, about DRAM's 864 nm2, at far lower capex and no EUV.
note: Hardwired-weight inference (via ROM) exists; inflexible to model updates.

title: Tire retreading: CXL rehab buffer gives retired DRAM second life
idea: Truck fleets retread tires instead of buying new. Sell a CXL memory-expander buffer chip whose periphery profiles retired DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs in situ (per-row retention margin, weak-column sensing), applies per-region refresh rates and column remaps, and pools them as tier-2 memory under strong ECC, fed by hyperscaler decommissioning streams.
why: Water/supply: a reused GB avoids essentially all of its manufacturing water (>10x vs new) and adds supply with no fab; large volumes of retired DRAM are shredded today.

title: Reverse fab: harvest, retest and rebin retired server DRAM
idea: First principle: DRAM has effectively unlimited endurance and no dominant wear-out, so a 5-year-old die is physically almost as good as new. Build automated lines that desolder DRAM packages from retired DIMMs and boards, reball them, run full BIST, retention and row-hammer binning, and assemble certified second-life modules.
why: Supply: hyperscalers retire many exabytes of DRAM per year; recovered bits cost ~5% of new-fab capex per bit and arrive in months.

title: Overbuild 120 tiers, fuse to 100: tier-level sparing
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: deliberately deposit ~20% more tiers than the product needs, add a per-block tier-remap register, and e-fuse out any tier that fails test (shorts, Vt outliers, weak capacitors). The process window can then be loosened (faster deposition, cheaper precursors) because whole-tier defects become yield-neutral.
why: Fact 2: turns compounding tier loss (0.99^100 ~ 37% yield) into >90% die yield, cutting 3D cost per bit ~2x at a fixed defect density.

title: Core-rope via-programmed 3D weight store, one sense per rope
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope, where a bit was set by whether a wire threaded a core: inference weights are encoded by whether a BEOL via links a rope wire to a shared sense node, written by maskless laser/e-beam via patterning in a mature U.S. fab and stacked 16 metal decks high, with one sense amp per 64 rope wires. Static weights leave DRAM, which keeps only activations and KV cache.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: weights are often >50% of inference DRAM; rope bits cost ~5-10x less than DRAM bits and need no EUV, capacitor or refresh.

title: HP's The Machine fixed: pooled memory racks with a refurbishment loop
idea: HPE's The Machine died betting on an unready memristor. Build the same memory-centric fabric with today's DRAM in CXL-attached pooled racks, sold as a service. Modules are hot-swapped, tested, refurbished and redeployed to lower tiers instead of retiring with the server.
why: Pooling cuts stranded DRAM (often 20-40% unused per server), and refurbishment roughly doubles module life, raising usable supply without new fabs.
note: CXL pooling widely pursued.

title: Minify embedding tables to hash encoders plus tiny MLPs
idea: Minify TB-scale recommender embedding tables into multi-hash encoders plus a small MLP that computes each embedding on the fly on tensor cores (deep hash embedding), with no stored rows.
why: Embedding memory falls 100x+, and recommender inference, a top consumer of server DRAM, needs >=10x less of it.
note: Embeddings computed not stored could cut recommender DRAM 10x+; DHE/TT-Rec prior art, doubt is compute cost and accuracy at scale.

title: Vinyl-record pressing: via-programmed mask ROM for frozen model weights
idea: Borrowed from record pressing, where one stamper makes millions of discs: frozen model weights are pressed into 1-transistor mask ROM by a single cheap via/metal mask on a commodity logic wafer (no EUV, no capacitor) stacked under the accelerator, so weights need zero DRAM and zero refresh; a new model version is a new via mask.
why: Removes the weight footprint from DRAM; mask ROM is dense, has zero standby and refresh power, uses mature U.S.-available nodes and needs no capacitor or EUV.

title: Minify replica count: consolidate long-tail models by global routing
idea: Minify how many places each model's weights must be resident: a global router concentrates all traffic for each long-tail model onto the fewest replicas that meet the SLO, and cold models page in from NVMe in under a second.
why: Pinned weight DRAM for fleets of thousands of models falls >=10x, which turns DRAM spend into a scheduling problem.
note: ServerlessLLM-style routing and fast loading known.

title: Minify graphs with gap-coded adjacency and hardware decoder
idea: Minify web and social graph adjacency using WebGraph-style reference copying, gap and zeta coding. A near-memory decoder streams neighbor lists at line rate to the graph engine.
why: Graph analytics needs 10-20x less memory per edge, so trillion-edge graphs fit in one rack.

title: Demoscene 64k coder: neural texture compression plugin for game engines
idea: Demosceners fit whole worlds in 64 KB. An Unreal/Godot plugin encodes each material's texture stack (albedo, normal, roughness and more) into a small latent grid plus a tiny MLP decoded in the shader at sample time, replacing block-compressed mip chains. A 4-person team can build it in 24 months.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game and VR memory. Neural textures give 4-8x over BCn, letting consoles, PCs and headsets ship with less DRAM.
note: NVIDIA NTC already exists; engine plugin is an execution play.

title: IBM MXT, fixed: compression moved behind CXL where latency is free
idea: MXT (2000) compressed all memory in 1 KB sectors behind a 32 MB L3, so every miss paid decompression and the extra cache chip cost more than the DRAM saved. Put an LZ4/zstd engine inside a CXL Type-3 expander that already costs ~150-250 ns, compress at 4 KB with a 64 MB uncompressed hot-line buffer, and expose 2-3x physical capacity as plain memory.
why: Cost per bit: 2-3x effective GB in the far tier; decompression hides inside the existing CXL hop, removing the latency and cost penalty that killed MXT.
note: Being commercialized (e.g. CXL compressed-memory controllers).

title: Host-DRAM-lite AI servers decode data shards directly on GPU
idea: IFR: AI-server host memory shrinks to almost nothing. Constraint: adding no new chips means adding no scarce elements, so delete host DRAM's jobs instead: compressed training shards go storage-to-GPU and are decoded by GPU kernels, and checkpoints stream GPU-to-NVMe directly, removing the staging buffers that justify 1-2 TB per node.
why: Host DRAM per AI node drops from ~2 TB to ~256 GB, an 8x cut on a large slice of server DRAM bought today.
note: GPUDirect Storage and GPU decode already exist.

title: Semantic snapshots: background apps keep only re-creatable state
idea: Imposed limit: a background phone app gets 2 MB. The OS makes each app serialize a semantic snapshot (navigation stack, form inputs, scroll positions, auth tokens) and then discards its heap; on relaunch the app rehydrates from the snapshot and a cached UI layout instead of restoring the whole heap.
why: Phones ship 12-16 GB mainly to keep apps warm; semantic snapshots could keep the same perceived warmth at 6-8 GB, and phones take roughly a third of all DRAM bits.
note: Android saved-instance-state already does this; adoption and perceived warmth are the hurdles.

title: Swap fp32 vector-index embeddings for 1-bit codes plus SSD rerank
idea: Substitute full-precision vectors in DRAM with sign-bit codes. Vector databases keep only binary codes in DRAM for Hamming-distance candidate search (popcount on existing CPUs) and read the fp32 vectors of the top ~100 candidates from NVMe to rerank.
why: Billion-vector RAG and search indexes shrink ~25x in DRAM at about a 1-point recall loss, with unchanged DDR.
note: Binary codes plus rerank already standard in vector DBs.

title: Swap greedy tensor allocators for ILP-planned rematerialization and packing
idea: Substitute runtime greedy allocation with a solved plan. One integer program over the training graph decides jointly which activations to keep, recompute or offload and their exact arena offsets, removing fragmentation and peak-coincident lifetimes before the run.
why: Training peak memory falls 2-4x versus caching allocators with heuristic checkpointing, for ~10-20% extra compute, on unchanged HBM.

title: Swap stored embedding rows for IDs hashed through a tiny MLP
idea: Substitute lookup with generation. Recommendation models replace multi-TB ID embedding tables with deep hash embeddings: k hash functions turn each ID into a dense code, a small shared MLP produces the embedding on the fly, and exact rows are kept only for the hottest 1% of IDs.
why: Embedding tables dominate recommendation DRAM, and generating rows cuts them 10-100x at small accuracy cost on unchanged servers.
note: Deep Hash Embedding is published prior art.

title: Datacenter-wide prompt-prefix KV cache on flash servers
idea: Combine content-addressed storage with LLM prefill: KV blocks for common prefixes (system prompts, documents, tool schemas) are hashed by token sequence and stored once on NAND-heavy cache servers, and inference GPUs fetch matching prefix blocks over RDMA instead of recomputing them or pinning them in HBM.
why: Deduplicates the large share of KV repeated across users, cutting per-GPU KV footprint and prefill compute, built entirely from DUV-made NAND and mature networking.
note: Mooncake, LMCache and CachedAttention already do this.

title: Minify vector-DB residency to 1-bit codes plus flash rerank
idea: Minify every resident embedding to a binary sign code (32x smaller than FP32). Candidates are found by popcount Hamming search in DRAM and reranked with full-precision vectors fetched from NVMe.
why: Vector databases hold 32x more vectors per GB of DRAM at near-equal recall.

title: Eliminate full fine-tune copies with 1-bit deltas over shared bases
idea: Store each fine-tuned variant as the sign of its weight delta plus per-row scales relative to one resident base model, served by a fused dequant-add GPU kernel; it is a software product.
why: Serving 100 variants needs about 1.1x base memory instead of 100x, a 10-16x saving per variant.

title: Snapshot-and-restore replaces warm serverless sandbox pools
idea: Reverse 'keep warm' into 'keep cold, restore fast': idle function sandboxes are snapshotted to NVMe and restored in ~5-10 ms by lazily faulting in only the pages the first invocation touches, instead of holding thousands of warm VMs in DRAM.
why: Warm pools often leave 50-80% of serverless DRAM idle; replacing them cuts that DRAM 3-5x in software alone.
note: Firecracker snapshots, REAP and FaaSnap already do this.

title: Cheap short-living objects: retired server DDR4 reborn as CXL memory
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Collect, retest and bin them, then mount 8-16 on each CXL Type-3 card built around a 28 nm controller, as a cheap cold tier for KV cache and page cache. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Usable supply: reuses DRAM that already exists, at ~10-20% of new DRAM cost per GB and zero wafer starts.

title: Piggy bank: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn on CXL expander cards
idea: The 'piggy bank' of savings is the DDR4 sitting in decommissioned servers. Design a PCIe/CXL card around an off-the-shelf CXL memory controller ASIC that hosts 8 used DDR4 RDIMMs, plus a burn-in and test flow, and sell it as a capacity tier. Board design and pilot runs fit within $1M.
why: Cost per bit and supply: reused bits cost roughly 10-20% of new DDR5 and need zero new wafers.
note: Already deployed by hyperscalers (CXL DDR4 reuse); straightforward but not novel.

title: Ternary weights packed five trits per byte with LUT decode
idea: Box: representation shrink × model training × weights × train time × 3^5 = 243 states in 8 bits + table decode. Models trained natively ternary store five weights per byte and decode via a 256-entry table held in registers or shared memory.
why: 1.6 bits per weight versus 16 is a 10× weight-memory cut, achieved with algorithms and existing GPUs only, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Hashing-trick embedding tables at 1% size
idea: Worsen: keep a dedicated row for every user and item ID in TB-scale embedding tables. Flip: hash IDs into a table 100x smaller with multiple hash functions and train with collisions, adding a tiny per-ID sign or scale to separate colliding IDs.
why: Cost: 100x less DRAM for recommendation embeddings; trades small accuracy loss.

title: Keyword-spotter extreme: ternary weights stored as zero-skipping trit runs
idea: From always-on keyword spotters that run ternary networks: models are trained to {-1, 0, +1} weights stored as base-3 packed trits (5 per byte) with run-length skip lists for zeros, decoded by adder-only compute units that skip zero runs.
why: About 1.6 bits per weight or less versus 16 is a 10x+ cut in weight DRAM/HBM, and fab water falls proportionally.

title: Cobalt kobold miners: tiny SRAM index picks which KV pages to fetch
idea: Cobalt is named for the kobold that hunted ore; each 16-token KV page gets a 64-byte summary (per-channel key min/max) in SRAM, decode computes upper-bound attention scores from the summaries and fetches only the top 3-5% of pages from DRAM, while the rest of the KV lives in CXL memory or NAND.
why: Per-token KV traffic falls 20-30x (well over 10x lower energy per access), and the HBM/DRAM KV footprint shrinks to the hot pages with the long tail in cheaper flash (energy, cost/bit).

title: Datacenter-wide prefix radix tree deduplicates shared KV across users
idea: IFR: identical context is cached once for the planet. Closest with no materials: a cluster-wide radix tree keyed by token prefixes stores shared KV blocks (system prompts, popular documents, few-shot examples) once per pod, and requests are routed to the pod holding their longest prefix.
why: Shared prefixes are 30-70% of tokens in many products; that share of KV is deduplicated.

title: Cascade router sends easy queries to small models first
idea: IFR: every query is answered with the smallest memory possible. Closest with no hardware: a confidence-calibrated cascade routes queries to a 3B model (6 GB) first and escalates to the 400B model only when a verifier flags uncertainty, so fewer replicas of the giant model are needed.
why: If 70% of traffic stays small, giant-model replicas and their HBM drop ~3x.
note: FrugalGPT/RouteLLM are prior art.

title: Thermally drawn fiber preforms yield coaxial capacitor bundles
idea: Adapt optical-fiber drawing: build a macroscopic preform of metal/glass/metal coaxial rods, draw it ~1000x down to 30 nm features over km lengths, slice it into thin wafers of parallel coaxial capacitors, and hybrid-bond them onto access-transistor wafers.
why: Facts 1 and 4: any aspect ratio for the price of drawing glass, with no HAR etch or EUV in the capacitor; registration to transistors is the main risk.
note: Capacitor length becomes slice thickness, decoupling AR from etch; registration and 30 nm draw breakup are doubts.

title: Turbine-blade eutectic solidification grows built-in vertical nanorod plates
idea: Borrowed from directionally solidified eutectic alloys used in turbine blades: solidify a Si-TaSi2 eutectic ingot so billions of aligned metallic TaSi2 nanorods run through monocrystalline Si, then slice wafers in which each rod is a ready-made vertical capacitor plate or buried bitline, with cells formed around them by one mask.
why: Self-organized vertical conductors replace high-AR etch and fill (facts 1,4); a ~100x path if fast growth brings rod pitch near ~100 nm; trade-off: irregular lattice needs per-die mapping.
note: Self-organized eutectic rods as pre-built vertical plates is unseen; rod pitch is microns at practical growth rates.

title: Eliminate storage-node lithography: transistors electroplate their own capacitor towers
idea: Eliminate the storage-node mask and etch: after building the access transistors, immerse the wafer in a plating bath and turn on every wordline so each working transistor's drain contact sources current and plates its own Ni/Ru nanotower; then add ALD dielectric (N2 purge) and top plate. No argon-sputtered seed is needed because the drains are the seeds.
why: Self-aligned capacitor with no litho layer and no etch (fact 4); towers reach AR 100+ by plating time (fact 1); dead transistors grow no node, giving a built-in yield screen; risk is plating uniformity across billions of sites.
note: Transistors plate their own nodes: self-aligned, mask-free, built-in yield screen; free-standing AR-100 towers will lean and collapse.

title: Vertical plated-wire memory: NiFe-lined holes through word-plane stack
idea: Revive 1960s plated-wire memory (NiFe electroplated on beryllium-copper wire, non-destructive readout, flown in Apollo-era and Skylab systems): etch vertical holes through an epitaxial stack of heavily doped silicon word planes by metal-assisted chemical etching, electroplate a circumferentially magnetized NiFe film on each hole wall around a copper core, and store a bit where each word plane crosses a hole. A word current tilts the magnetization slightly and the core senses the induced voltage without destroying it.
why: Facts 2 and 8: a 3D array from one critical hole mask using only aqueous etch and plating (no rare gas), with readout that avoids destructive read and writeback. Risks are mV-level read signal below 100 nm and word-plane selectivity.
note: 3D NDRO magnetic memory from one hole mask is new; inductive read signal collapses at sub-100 nm.

title: Light-pumped self-restoring cell: photodiode gated by its own charge
idea: Box: cap x Si access nMOS x SA x backside-illuminated die under a uniform LED/laser sheet x thinned Si x BSI image-sensor process. Each cell adds a photodiode in series with a tiny transistor gated by the storage node, so a global light flash tops up only nodes that are already high, refreshing the whole array in parallel without any row activation.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3) moves from ~46 fJ/bit bitline CV2 to a few fJ/bit of photons with zero activations, also removing refresh-driven hammer (fact 9). Stray photocurrent into 0-nodes is the risk.
note: Light-driven, self-gated top-up refreshes the whole array with zero activations; doubts: photodiode area per cell, stray photocurrent into 0-nodes.

title: Millefiori glass-cane draw sliced into litho-free vertical access arrays
idea: Assemble a cm-scale preform holding ~10^4 coaxial access-transistor cross-sections (chalcogenide-glass semiconductor core, glass gate dielectric, low-melting metal gate). Thermally draw it 10^4x as Venetian millefiori cane or optical fiber is drawn, then slice 100 nm discs: each slice is a ready-made array of vertical gate-all-around access switches.
why: Capital intensity and fact 4: removes the EUV patterning of the access layer altogether. A wide-gap glassy channel gives low off-current, and one draw tower replaces scanners for this layer.
note: Multimaterial fiber draw (Fink lab) sliced into GAA access arrays; doubts: 10 nm uniformity, chalcogenide channel quality, contacting slices.

title: Advance market commitment for next-generation memory bits
idea: Combine the vaccine Advance Market Commitment model with memory. Governments and hyperscalers pre-commit to buy the first 10 EB of any DRAM-class technology that meets $/GB, latency and endurance thresholds, at a guaranteed premium price that tapers.
why: Removes the demand-risk valley of death for 3D DRAM, gain-cell or capacitorless entrants. That pulls new tech and new fabs forward by years.
note: AMC model applied to new memory tech; addresses entrant demand-risk valley.

title: Eliminate the incumbents' data monopoly: open 1-um access-device PDK across universities
idea: Publish an open process kit for 100 mm wafer access devices (Si, SiC, Ga2O3 variants) runnable in ten U.S. university nanofabs, each running monthly shuttles with standardized retention-tail test structures; pooled data on millions of cells reveal which elimination (junction, oxide, body) shrinks the tail.
why: Breaks the barrier that only three firms see leakage-tail statistics at scale; accelerates U.S. access-device innovation for ~$10M/yr instead of a $15B fab.

title: Matchstick: consume-once reads with decoupled sense amps skip restore
